When I read the Master’s "Text Encouraging the Arousing of Bodhicitta," I could not help but feel sweat drench my back and tears moisten my robes.

Long ago, when our World-Honored One first attained perfect enlightenment, he sighed, saying: "How marvelous! How marvelous! There is not a single sentient being who does not possess [the Buddha-nature]."
The wisdom of the Tathāgata cannot be realized because of false conceptualization, inversion, and attachment.
If one is free from false conceptualization, then all-knowledge, spontaneous knowledge, and unimpeded knowledge will manifest before one.

I simply do not understand why these sentient beings, despite their false conceptualizations and attachments, find it so painful not to abandon them; and why they have such dread toward the wisdom of the Tathāgata.
He did not realize it; in the end, he abandoned his father and fled, drifting for long kalpas and contentedly serving as a lowly laborer, unaware of how to return.
This was due to nothing other than a lack of awareness. The bodhicitta is simply another name for this very awareness.
The moment one realizes this, the deluded thoughts and attachments manifesting before one are entirely the wisdom of the Tathāgata. For the wisdom of the Tathāgata has no separate substance;
it takes the deluded thoughts of sentient beings as its substance. The deluded thoughts of sentient beings have no separate substance;

they take the wisdom of the Tathāgata as their substance. It is like water forming waves: the waves are entirely water. From the very beginning, they have ultimately and eternally abided in the state of non-remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
Because of *nirvāṇa*. Nevertheless, the distinction between awakening and non-awakening is something one must by no means deceive oneself about or remain ignorant of.
If one reflects with sudden alertness here and attains understanding with a swift clarity, then the arousal of the *bodhicitta* will naturally flow forth with irresistible force.
Once this mind has been aroused, what further need is there for all-knowledge, natural knowledge, or unimpeded knowledge?
How extraordinary! This Master was born during the twilight of the Dharma-ending age; yet, upon beholding the śarīra relics, he suddenly gave rise to the Great Mind.
Throughout his life, his conduct was in accordance with the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* and his aspiration was fixed upon the Western Land.

To express this, he laid bare his heart and exposed his liver—a sincerity so profound that even the metaphors of "rescuing those from fire" or "saving those drowning" fall short. He was truly a banner of diligence for the Dharma-ending age. Formerly, Sudhana...
The youth traveled extensively to consult various spiritual teachers (*kalyāṇamitra*). First, he attained fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) from Mañjuśrī;
subsequently, he met Meghashri and heard the dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation (*buddhānusmṛti*). At his passing, Samantabhadra guided him back to Sukhāvatī by means of the ten great kings of vows.
When one examines the Master’s aspirations and deeds, how could they not coincide with those of the Great Being of the *Avataṃsaka* without prior consultation? Some say that [this was] Bodhi...
The one who has raised their mind [to enlightenment] pervades all places. What wise person would wish for the East or the West? Answer:

Ordinary beings with great aspiration have just entered the Dharma-realm but have not yet realized the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*). Having once passed through the prison of the womb, they immediately lose awareness of their former causes.

How could this compare to being entrusted to a lotus pedestal, forever free from the cycle of birth and death (*saṃvartanī-kalpa*), hearing the Dharma and attaining the fruit, manifesting bodies everywhere to respond to beings, serving the Buddhas above and... [serving sentient beings below].
To deliver sentient beings until they reach nirvana, never again to regress—this is a matter of benefit and harm as distinct as heaven and abyss.
Furthermore, you claim that the bodhicitta pervades all places; if this were so, then moving from east to west would be like the extension and contraction of a single arm.
Within the context of a single body, one might prefer its contraction over its extension. Can this truly be called...?
How wise! Alas! The Master now departs; though empty space may come to an end, my vow shall never cease. How could the Master’s heart ever reach its limit?
May those who read this record be able to aspire to the Master’s aspirations and practice the Master’s deeds.
This means that it is appropriate for the Master to manifest his body and preach the Dharma; I shall spread my hair to receive his feet and scatter various fragrant flowers upon that spot.

This *Collected Works of Dharma Master Sheng’an* is truly a provision for the cultivation of the Pure Land and a treasure of the Buddha-remembrance dharma-gate.
This is a raft. It is a pity that this book is not commonly seen; after the ravages of war, its printing blocks have long since vanished, and the text itself has become impossible to obtain.
Now, having happened upon this copy at the residence of a friend, both monastics and laypeople alike delight in reciting it.
Therefore, I wish to publish and distribute it widely. Fortunately, I have encountered [this opportunity].
Shouyuan Fu Chenjun and Gengen Fu Zhangjun share the same aspiration as I; they have thus acted as the initiators.

Together with all their fellow practitioners who believe in the good, they have joyfully consented to have this work carved into printing blocks, so that the single lineage of the Lotus School may be propagated.

They shall arise in continuous succession, never to be severed. All practitioners of the Pure Land path must strictly follow the rules established by the Patriarchs and place firm faith in the guidance of the Bequeathed Teachings.
These instructions are most detailed and most earnest; though the language is simple, it is easy to understand.
What is proximate is easy to follow. This book is exceptionally difficult to obtain; therefore, I have specially commissioned a wide printing and sent it forth everywhere.

I only wish that my fellow practitioners and dharma companions will joyfully read this book, receive and uphold it according to the Dharma, and attain birth in the Pure Land, so that all those with faith throughout the world who hear of it may clasp their hands in joy and exultation.

The *Bequeathed Letters of Master Sheng’an* are a work that transmits the orthodox lineage of the Lotus School (Lotus Sect). Master Haiyun has re-carved them;
having obtained them through the practice of Pure Land, he has rectified the root and clarified the source—his merit is truly great.

I have further requested that the complete transmission from the First Patriarch of the Lotus School to the Ninth Patriarch be published. This coincides with his intention, and I thus entrust him with adding a few words to strengthen its preservation.
I hold this view. Thus, I shall set forth my humble observations: The Lotus School is the orthodox tradition; it is the authentic teaching.
When a student attains it, they become as straight as wood following a plumb line. However, whether a student attains it or not depends solely on their fortune or misfortune.
If fortunate, one rectifies the will and mind, thereby naturally attaining the correct learning. If unfortunate, one fails to attain that correctness, and calamity ensues.

It must reach one's own person. What is called "cultivating the person" lies in rectifying the mind; there has never been a case where the mind was not rectified and yet the person could be cultivated.

Since you, O Chan Master, have fortunately attained the orthodox transmission, you further wish to skillfully lead others to attain it as well, so that they may together hear the correct words and together return to the right path.
Excellent, excellent! You are one who first perfects oneself and subsequently benefits others universally. It is just as [the sages] said: [The original text concludes with: "...as if... (如).

If all people were to align their hearts with one another, correcting themselves and correcting others, so that all attain the fruit of perfection, how could there be anyone in the world who is unfortunate?
Having finished writing this, all the myriad sounds fell silent; the full moon hung in the sky, and I further composed a verse: Heaven and earth are like an inn;
All people are but passing travelers. Only the mind of the sages and worthies Shines eternally, like the sun and moon.

Master Shěng’ān was the sole successor to the Great Master Liánchí; thus he is called the Ninth Patriarch of the Lotus School.

Throughout a thousand years, past and present, there have been only nine such individuals. All were accomplished through the path of the "gentleman-scholar" (*junzǐrú*) and became patriarchs of the Lotus School. Each of them...

His biographies and writings have been transmitted through the ages. Regarding the three teachings of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism, he attained the correct essence of each and achieved merit in all of them;

how could it be said that he was merely a fortunate addition to the Buddhist school alone? As for the Dharma Master’s posthumous letters, poetry, and prose, they clarify Confucianism through an understanding of Buddhism and expound Buddhism in support of Confucianism;

furthermore, they provide instructions on the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha's name) and the cultivation of the Pure Land, emphasizing the principle of "single-mindedness and exclusive devotion."
Extremely concise and lucid, it is truly a compassionate vessel for the sea of suffering and a precious raft for those lost on the path.

Because the text was rarely seen following the wars and the printing blocks no longer existed, the Chan Master Zhongning Haiyun of Hangzhou urgently sought to have it re-engraved and widely disseminated.
It is like holding a candle while traveling at night, or pointing out the way for one who has lost their path. I rejoice in assisting him to fulfill his aspirations.
Through this, people may trace back to the source and flow, together returning to perfect enlightenment; they shall again clarify the fundamental essence and all obtain the true exposition.
It will be seen that the lineage of the Lotus School shall continue its succession, with no lack of worthy successors from generation to generation.
That heterodox paths and deviant doctrines shall, for the most part, fail to delude the world—is this not the supreme fortune of our own kind and the high expectation of the Ninth Patriarch?

I pray that the men and women of this world who possess pure faith will, out of compassion, deign to lend me their attention for a moment. I have often heard that the essential gateway to entering the Way is to take the arousal of the bodhicitta as primary;
that cultivation is the urgent task, and the establishment of vows is the foremost priority. Once the vow is established, sentient beings can be delivered.

When the mind is awakened, the Buddha-way can be accomplished. If one does not give rise to the vast and great mind and establish firm vows, then even if one passes through kalpas as numerous as dust motes, one will still remain within saṃsāra;
though one may engage in practice, it will all be nothing but fruitless toil and hardship. Therefore, the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
"To forget the bodhicitta while practicing various wholesome dharmas is called the work of Māra. If this is so when one has already forgotten it, how much more so when one has never given rise to it!
How much more so for those who have not yet resolved their minds? Therefore, one should know that those who wish to study the Tathāgata-yāna must first fully resolve upon the bodhisattva vow;
this must not be delayed. However, as the distinctions within these mental vows are manifold, if they are not specifically set forth, how can one proceed toward them?

Now, for the sake of the great assembly, I shall speak of them briefly. There are eight such aspects, namely: the deviant and the correct, the true and the false, the Great and the Small, and the partial and the universal.
"Perfect" (*yuan*) refers to this. What are called "deviant and correct," "true and false," "great and small," "partial and perfect"?

In the world there are practitioners who practice exclusively in a one-sided manner, failing to investigate their own minds and knowing only external affairs; they either seek profit and sustenance or crave fame and reputation.
If one generates the mind [of awakening] out of greed for the pleasures of the present life, or with the hope for future karmic rewards, such a resolve is called "erroneous.
Since it seeks neither gain, offerings, nor fame, nor is it greedy for the fruits of sensual pleasure, but aims solely for the sake of *saṃsāra* and for *bodhi*, such a resolve is called "correct.
In every thought-moment, one seeks the Buddha-way above; in every mind, one transforms sentient beings below.

Having given rise [to the aspiration], one hears that the Buddha-way is long and distant, yet does not give way to discouragement; one observes that sentient beings are difficult to deliver, yet does not give way to weariness.
It is like ascending a mountain ten thousand fathoms high—one must reach its summit; like climbing a nine-storied pagoda—one must reach its pinnacle.

To resolve the mind in this manner is called "true. If there is sin one does not repent, or a fault one does not eliminate, being turbid within while appearing pure without—this is merely the beginning.
Diligence ends in indolence. Though one possesses a good heart, it is mostly intermingled with fame and profit; though one possesses wholesome dharmas, they are further defiled by sinful karma.
To resolve the mind in such a manner is called "false. Only when the realm of sentient beings is exhausted shall my vow be exhausted;
only when the path to Bodhi is accomplished shall my vow be accomplished. To resolve the mind in such a manner is called "great. Contemplate this.

To regard the three realms as a prison and to view birth and death as an enemy, aspiring only to deliver oneself while having no desire to deliver others—such a resolution of the mind is called "small.

If one perceives sentient beings and the Buddha-way as existing outside of the mind, vowing to deliver them and achieve enlightenment while not forgetting one's own merit or allowing one's knowledge and vision to perish—such a resolution of the mind is called "partial. If...
Knowing that the self-nature is sentient beings, one vows to deliver them. Knowing that the self-nature is the Buddha-way, one vows to achieve it.

One does not perceive a single dharma that exists apart from the mind. With a mind as empty as space, one makes a vow as empty as space, practices conduct as empty as space, and realizes a fruit as empty as space;
yet even the mark of emptiness is unattainable. To arouse the mind in this manner is called...
This constitutes its circularity. To know these eight kinds of distinctions is to know how to investigate; to know how to investigate is to know how to adopt or reject;
to know how to adopt or reject is to be able to resolve the mind toward awakening. How does one investigate? It means: regarding the mind I have resolved to awaken, among these eight [categories]...
Is it deviant or correct? Is it true or false? Is it great or small? Is it partial or perfect? How does one choose between them? That is to say:
abandon the deviant, abandon the false, abandon the small, and abandon the partial; adopt the correct, adopt the true, adopt the great, and adopt the perfect.
Only by generating the mind in this manner can it be called the genuine generation of the bodhicitta. Among all virtues, this bodhicitta—
"O King, there must be causes and conditions for such a thought to arise. Now, these causes and conditions are briefly of ten kinds. What are the ten?
First, because of mindfulness of the Buddha’s profound kindness; second, because of mindfulness of the kindness of one's parents; third, because of mindfulness of teachers and elders..."

First, out of gratitude for [the Buddha’s] kindness; second, out of gratitude for the kindness of one’s parents; third, out of gratitude for the kindness of all sentient beings; fourth, out of mindfulness of the kindness of donors;

fifth, out of mindfulness of the kindness of all sentient beings; sixth, out of mindfulness of the suffering of birth and death; seventh, out of reverence for one’s own spirit; eighth, out of repentance for karmic obstructions;

ninth, out of the desire to be born in the Pure Land; tenth, for the sake of mindfulness so that the True Dharma may endure for a long time. What is meant by mindfulness of the Buddha’s profound kindness?
It is said that I, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, first resolved to attain enlightenment for the sake of beings such as ourselves.

For immeasurable eons, I practiced the bodhisattva path and underwent all manner of sufferings. When I was creating karma, the Buddha felt compassion and used skillful means to teach and transform me;

yet, being ignorant and deluded, I did not know how to believe and accept his guidance. When I fell into hell, the Buddha again felt profound sorrow and wished to take my suffering upon himself; however, I—
My karma is heavy; I could not be rescued or uplifted. Though I was born into the human realm, the Buddha used skillful means to cause me to plant roots of goodness.

From life to life and birth after birth, [these roots] have followed me, never abandoning my mind for even a moment. When the Buddha first appeared in the world, I was still submerged in the depths of suffering;
now that I have obtained a human body, the Buddha has already entered parinirvāṇa. By what sin was I born in this Dharma-ending age? By what merit did I join the monastic order? What obstacles...
Yet I did not behold the Golden Body. How fortunate that I have personally encountered the śarīra! Reflecting thus, I thought:
had I not planted roots of goodness, how could I have heard the Buddha-dharma? Had I not heard the Buddha-dharma, how could I have known that I constantly receive the Buddha’s grace?

This grace and this virtue are as difficult to compare to as a mountain or a heap of earth. Were it not for giving rise to the vast mind, practicing the bodhisattva path, and establishing the Buddha-dharma, [this would not be possible].
To save and deliver sentient beings—even at the cost of grinding one’s bones to powder and shattering one’s body—how could one ever repay them?
This is the foremost cause and condition for generating the bodhicitta. How does one contemplate the kindness of one's parents? Alas, my parents! Their toil in bringing me forth was profound.

For ten months and three years they carried me in the womb and nursed me with milk. They pushed aside the dry to take the wet, swallowed the bitter while spitting out the sweet. Only then did I attain human form. Pointing [at me], they said...

We hope that you will continue the family tradition and maintain the ancestral sacrifices. Now that we have already left the household life, we falsely claim the title of Śākyaputra and shamefully bear the name of śramaṇa;
yet we do not provide them with fine delicacies, nor do we provide for their ritual offerings and grave-sweeping.

We cannot nourish their physical bodies while they live, nor can we guide their spiritual essence after death. This is a great detriment to the world and offers no true benefit to the transcendental realm.

Since both paths have been lost, grave offenses are difficult to escape. Reflecting thus, one realizes that only by constantly practicing the Buddha-way throughout hundreds of kalpas and thousands of lifetimes—universally delivering sentient beings across the ten directions and the three periods of time—can not only the parents of this single life be saved, but all parents of every lifetime be delivered;
not only the parents of this single person, but the parents of every individual be enabled to transcend and ascend. This is...
This is the second cause and condition for generating the bodhicitta. What is meant by "mindfulness of the kindness of teachers and elders"?
Although one's parents can give birth to and raise one's body, if there were no worldly teachers and elders, one would not know propriety and righteousness;

if there were no supramundane teachers and elders, one would not understand the Buddha-dharma. If one does not know propriety and righteousness, one is the same as other species; if one does not understand the Buddha-dharma, then...

"How are we any different from worldly people? Now we have a rough knowledge of propriety and righteousness; we have a basic understanding of the Buddha-dharma; the *kāṣāya* robe covers our bodies, and the precepts drench our persons.
This profound kindness was obtained from our teachers and elders. If we were to seek only the small fruits [of the Hīnayāna], we could merely benefit ourselves.
But now, for the sake of the Mahāyāna, we universally vow to benefit others; thus, both types of teachers—those of this world and those of the supramundane—will equally receive our benefit."
This is the third causal condition for generating the bodhicitta. What is meant by "mindfulness of the benefactor's kindness"?

It means that all the provisions we currently use daily do not belong to ourselves. Whether it be the morning and evening meals throughout the three periods of the day, the clothing for the four seasons, the necessities during illness, or the expenses for body and speech—all of these originate from the power of others and are provided for our use; they are obtained through their diligent efforts.
Those who plow the fields with their own hands find it difficult even to sustain themselves; yet I sit at ease, receiving food while my heart remains unfulfilled.
They spin and weave without ceasing, still finding their lives arduous; yet I possess ample clothing and have no need to cherish them.

They dwell in huts with thatched doors and brushwood screens, struggling in turmoil until the end of their days; yet I reside in a spacious mansion with a tranquil courtyard, passing the year in leisurely ease. Compared to their toil...
To provide for my comfort and find peace of mind, and to use the benefit of others to nourish one's own person—is this consistent with principle?

Unless one possesses the dual movement of compassion and wisdom and the twofold adornment of merit and insight, such that donors receive grace and sentient beings receive gifts, then even a grain of rice or an inch of silk will result in a debt that must be repaid, and an evil retribution will be difficult to escape. This is the fourth causal condition for generating the bodhicitta.

What is meant by "mindfulness of the kindness of sentient beings"? It means that from time immemorial, throughout birth after birth and life after life, I and all sentient beings have been parents to one another;

thus, we have all bestowed kindness upon each other. Although we are now separated by lifetimes and, in our delusion, do not recognize one another, when we reason according to this principle, how could there not be a need for repayment?
How can those who now wear fur and carry horns not have been one's own children in the past? Now...
Among these wriggling and flying creatures, who knows that they have not once been my father?

When one observes those who separate from their parents in childhood and, upon reaching adulthood, completely forget their former countenances—how much more so for karmic relatives of past lives whose names and lineages are now difficult to recall?
While they wail beneath the hells and writhe among the hungry ghosts, who knows their agony? Who knows their hunger and emptiness?
I appeal to you. Although I have neither seen nor heard this myself, that person must surely seek rescue and salvation. It is not possible to set forth this matter except through the scriptures;
it is not possible to speak these words except through the Buddha. How could those people of false views be sufficient to know this?

Therefore, the Bodhisattva regards even ants as having all been his parents in the past and will become Buddhas in the future; he constantly contemplates their benefit and cherishes the thought of repaying their kindness.
This kindness constitutes the fifth causal condition for generating the bodhicitta. What is meant by "mindfulness of the suffering of birth and death"?
It means that I and all sentient beings have, since time immemorial, constantly existed within birth and death without attaining liberation, whether in the human realm or the heavens.

In this realm and in other quarters, beings emerge and vanish in myriad ways; they rise and sink in an instant. In one moment they are gods, in another humans, and in another hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts.
They leave the black gates in the morning and return by evening; they briefly depart from the iron caves only to enter them again.
When they ascend the mountain of blades, their entire bodies are stripped of skin; when they climb the tree of swords, their hearts are pierced.
All are torn asunder. Burning iron does not alleviate hunger; swallowing it causes the liver and intestines to rot away completely. Molten copper is no remedy for thirst;
drinking it causes the flesh and bones to be entirely ground to powder. Sharp saws dismember them, yet they are severed and then joined again. A clever wind blows upon them.
Then, having died, they are born again. Within the City of Fierce Flames, they endure the惨烈 cries of lamentation; upon the frying pans, they hear only the sounds of agonizing pain.
When the ice first freezes, their forms resemble the budding filaments of a blue lotus; when their flesh and blood are split apart, their bodies are like the blooming blossoms of a red lotus.
Dying and being reborn once a night, they pass through this subterranean realm ten thousand times each day. A single morning of such suffering—
Pain! A hundred years have already passed for humans; the wardens of hell are weary from their ceaseless toil. Who will believe the instructions of Lord Yama?
While suffering, one knows the pain and feels regret, yet what can be done to pursue liberation? Once released, one forgets it all again. One’s karmic actions remain as they were before:
when a donkey is whipped until it bleeds, who knows the grief of its mother? When a pig is led to the slaughter, who recognizes the agony of its father? To eat...
One’s own child and one does not know it; even King Wen was like this. Devouring one’s own kin without realization—this is the nature of all beings.
Those who were objects of affection in their prime have now become enemies; those who were foes in the past have now become flesh and bone.

She who was once one’s mother has now become one’s wife; he who was formerly one’s father has now become one’s husband. To know this through the power of past karma would be a cause for shame and disgrace. With the divine eye...
To look upon it, it is both laughable and pitiable. Amidst a mass of filth and excrement, it has been confined for ten months;
now, within a conduit of pus and blood, it collapses all at once—how pitiful! When young, what did one know? One could not distinguish east from west.
As one grew and gained consciousness, greed and desire arose. In an instant, old age and sickness followed in pursuit; in rapid succession, impermanence arrived. Wind and fire intermingle.
As it is fried, the spirit and consciousness within are thrown into turmoil. Once the vital essence and blood are exhausted, the skin and flesh wither from the outside.

There is not a single hair that has not been pierced by needles; there is not a single pore that has not been sliced open with a knife. For a tortoise about to be boiled, shedding its shell is still relatively easy;
yet for the spirit wishing to depart, its separation from the body is many times more difficult. The mind has no permanent master; it is like a merchant.
Yet one rushes about everywhere, the body having no fixed form; it is like a house that moves on and on from place to place.
The bodies that come and go are as numerous as the motes of dust throughout the great trichiliocosm; who can calculate the tears of parting shed amidst the waves of the four seas?
The towering piles of bones exceed those high mountains; the vast fields of scattered corpses outnumber the earth itself. Had one not heard the words of the Buddha, this...
Who has seen this? Who has heard it? Having not yet beheld the Buddhist scriptures, how could one know or perceive this principle?

If you continue to harbor attachments as before and remain mired in delusion as of old, I fear that for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, you will commit error after error. A human body is difficult to obtain and easy to lose;
a favorable time passes easily and is hard to recapture. The path ahead is dark and shrouded; parting shall be long-lasting, and the three evil realms await.
"Repaying [karma] means returning to receive it for oneself; the pain is beyond description. Who could take one's place? To bring such words to mind—how can one not feel a chill in the heart?
Therefore, one ought to sever the flow of birth and death and emerge from the ocean of craving and desire. To benefit both self and others, one must ascend together to the other shore.
This extraordinary merit across vast eons depends upon this single act. This is the sixth causal condition for generating the bodhicitta."
What is meant by honoring one’s own spirit? It means that my present single-mindedness is, directly and immediately, non-dual and indistinguishable from Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
How is it that while the World-Honored One attained perfect enlightenment long ago after immeasurable kalpas, we remain in confusion and delusion, still acting as ordinary beings?
Furthermore, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, possesses immeasurable supernatural powers and wisdom. His merit...
Their adornment is virtue, whereas we are merely bound by the fetters of immeasurable karma and afflictions, entangled in the cycle of birth and death.

The nature of the mind is one and the same; yet the difference between delusion and awakening is as vast as that between heaven and abyss. Reflecting on this in silence, how could it not be a cause for shame?
It is like a priceless jewel submerged in the mud, regarded as mere rubble and not treated with love or respect. Therefore, one ought to employ immeasurable...
When wholesome dharmas counteract the afflictions and the cultivation of virtue becomes efficacious, the innate qualities of one's nature will then manifest.

This is like a jewel that, having been washed and suspended upon a high banner, radiates a penetrating brilliance that outshines all else. One may then say that one has not failed the Buddha’s transformation nor betrayed one’s own spiritual nature;
this constitutes the seventh causal condition for generating the bodhicitta. How does one repent of karmic obstructions? As the Sūtra says:
Committing one *duṣkṛta* (minor offense) results in a lifespan of five hundred years in hell, equivalent to the lifespan of the Four Heavenly Kings.
If even such a minor offense as a *duṣkṛta* yields this retribution, how much more so for grave offenses? Their retribution is difficult to describe.

Now, within our daily lives, every movement and every gesture constantly violates the precepts; with every morsel of food and every sip of water, we repeatedly transgress the *śīla*. What has been committed in a single day—[is likewise...]
It should be immeasurable; how much more so the offenses committed throughout one's entire life across kalpas, which are truly beyond description.
To speak merely of the five precepts, nine out of ten people violate them; they are rarely confessed and mostly concealed. Yet these five precepts are called the *upāsaka* (lay follower) precepts.
They do not even fully possess these; how much less so the precepts of a śrāmaṇera, a bhikṣu, or a bodhisattva? It goes without saying.
When asked for their name, they say, "I am a bhikṣu. But when asked about the reality of it, they are not even fit to be upāsakas.
Is this not truly shameful? You should know that regarding the Buddha’s precepts, it is better not to receive them at all than to receive them and then violate them.
It is better not to violate them than to violate them; for if one violates them, one will inevitably fall into ruin.

Unless you take pity on yourself and others, and feel such grief for yourself and others that your body and mouth are overcome and your voice and tears flow together, seeking compassionate repentance on behalf of all sentient beings, then for thousands of births and myriad kalpas—
Evil retribution is difficult to escape. This constitutes the eighth causal condition for generating the bodhicitta. Why seek rebirth in the Pure Land?
It is said that practicing in this world makes progress on the Path difficult, whereas being reborn in that land makes the attainment of Buddhahood easy.

It is easy. Because it is easy, one lifetime suffices to attain it; because it is difficult [by other means], it remains unaccomplished even after kalpas. For this reason, the sages of antiquity and the worthies of former times all turned toward it;
throughout thousands of sutras and tens of thousands of treatises, everywhere it is pointed out as the ultimate destination. For those practicing in the Dharma-ending age, nothing surpasses this.
Yet the sutras state that few good deeds do not arise, but only through much merit is the goal reached. When we speak of "much merit," there is nothing better than upholding the Name.

Regarding the abundance of merit, nothing compares to giving rise to the vast and great mind (*mahācitta*). Therefore, even a momentary upholding of the Holy Name surpasses a hundred years of practicing generosity;
a single arousal of the great mind exceeds eons of cultivation. For the original purpose of recollecting the Buddha is to become a Buddha oneself.

If the great mind is not aroused, what is the use of recollecting him? The arousal of the mind is fundamentally for the sake of cultivation; if one is not born in the Pure Land, then even [if one has cultivated]... [what is the use]?
To resolve with ease is to retreat; this is the planting of the seed of Bodhi. To till it with the plow of mindfulness of the Buddha, the fruit of the Way will naturally increase.
Boarding the ship of great vows, one enters the ocean of the Pure Land; rebirth in the West is certain. This is the ninth causal condition for generating the Bodhicitta.
How does one cause the True Dharma to abide for a long time? It is said that our World-Honored One is without...
For immeasurable kalpas, for our sake, he cultivated the path to Bodhi; what was difficult to practice, he practiced; what was difficult to endure, he endured.
With causes perfected and fruits fulfilled, he eventually attained Buddhahood. Having attained Buddhahood, his transformative conditions having been fully exhausted, he entered Nirvana.

The True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma have both completely vanished, leaving only the Final Dharma. There are teachings but no people; the heterodox and the orthodox cannot be distinguished. This is...
It is not that there is no discernment; rather, people compete for "self" and "other," and all pursue profit and fame. Looking around, such people flow like a vast current; the whole world is thus.
They do not know who the Buddha is, what the Dharma means, or what the Sangha signifies. To have declined and wasted away to this point is almost beyond words.
Whenever I think of it, tears fall involuntarily. As a son of the Buddha, I am unable to repay his kindness; within me, there is no benefit.
To myself, I have been of no benefit; outwardly, I have not benefited others; in life, I have not benefited the present age; and in death, I shall not benefit those who come after.
Though heaven is high, it cannot cover me; though earth is thick, it cannot support me. If I am not the one guilty of the most grievous sins, then who is?
Because of this, my pain was unbearable and I saw no way out. Suddenly forgetting my own vulgarity and baseness, I abruptly gave rise to the Great Mind (*mahācitta*). Although I am unable—
At this time, we must turn back the final age of decline; we shall certainly strive to protect and uphold the True Dharma for future generations.
Therefore, together with our virtuous friends, we have come to this place of practice to perform repentance and establish this Dharma assembly.

We have made forty-eight great vows, vowing in each vow to deliver all living beings. With a profound resolve spanning hundreds of thousands of kalpas, we aspire in every thought-moment to attain Buddhahood. From this moment on...
Day by day, until the end of the future, exhausting this single lifetime, I vow to return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang).

Once I have attained the nine grades of rebirth, I shall return to the Sahā world so that the Sun of the Buddha may shine once more, the Dharma-gate may be proclaimed again, and the ocean of the Sangha may be made clear within this realm.
May the people of the Eastern Quarter be transformed by this teaching, the kalpas of the world’s duration be further extended, and the True Dharma be able to abide for a long time. This is the—
To distinguish the sincere and diligent efforts of the heart—this constitutes the tenth causal condition for generating the bodhicitta.
When these ten conditions are fully understood and the eight dharmas are thoroughly known, one will then approach the gateway of existence and find the ground for its development.

Having together attained this human body, dwelling in the land of the Middle Kingdom, with the six sense faculties unimpaired and the four elements in a state of light ease, and possessing faith, one is fortunately free from demonic interference.

How much more so now that we have been able to leave the household life, receive full ordination, encounter a site of enlightenment, hear the Buddha-dharma, behold the śarīra, practice the methods of repentance, meet virtuous friends, and possess such superior conditions?
If we do not give rise to this great resolve today, what day shall we wait for? We only pray that the great assembly will have compassion for our ignorant sincerity and pity our suffering.

We resolve together to establish this vow and together to give rise to this mind: those who have not yet given rise to it shall do so now; those who have already given rise to it shall cause it to increase;

and those who have already increased it shall now cause it to continue uninterrupted. Do not be intimidated by what is difficult and retreat in cowardice; do not regard what is easy and become frivolous;
do not desire quick results and fail to persevere for the long term; do not be indolent and lack vigor; and do not be despondent and fail to rouse yourselves.
Do not remain complacent and wait for the future; do not be consistently indifferent due to dullness and ignorance;
do not disparage yourself as lacking the capacity because your roots are shallow. It is like planting a tree: though the roots may be shallow at first, they grow deeper with time.

It is also like sharpening a blade: though the blade may be dull at first, it becomes keen through constant whetting. How can one refrain from planting simply because the roots are shallow, allowing the tree to wither away on its own? Because...
If dullness is not ground away, it is left useless. Furthermore, if one regards spiritual practice as suffering, one fails to realize that indolence is even more bitter.

Through practice, one exerts effort for a brief moment to attain peace and joy for eternal kalpas; through indolence, one steals a moment’s ease for this single lifetime only to suffer for many lifetimes.
How much more so when the Pure Land is taken as one's vessel—how could one worry about falling back? Moreover, one attains the realization of non-arising.
If one possesses the power of patience, what need is there to worry about hardships? One should know that even those who are sinners in the hells have given rise to the Bodhi-mind in past kalpas;
how much more so for us, as fellow human beings and sons of the Buddha, not to establish great vows in this present life?

Though the confusion of beginningless time cannot be remedied by those who have already passed away, since we have now awakened, it is still possible to catch up regarding the future. Nevertheless, while one remains deluded and has not yet awakened, it is indeed...
How pitiable! If one knows [the truth] yet fails to practice it, this is all the more cause for lamentation.
If one fears the suffering of the hells, diligence will arise spontaneously; if one contemplates the swiftness of impermanence, indolence will not arise.

Furthermore, one must take the Buddha-dharma as a whip and virtuous friends as guides, never parting from them even in moments of haste, relying on them for the rest of one's life; thus, there shall be no falling away.
Be cautious! Do not say that a single thought is trivial; do not claim that a sincere vow is of no benefit. When the mind is true, the reality is actualized;
when the vow is vast, the practice becomes profound. Space is not the greatest; the sovereign mind is the greatest. The diamond is not the hardest; the power of the vow is the hardest of all.

If the great assembly can truly not reject my words, then the kinship of Bodhi shall form a matrimonial alliance, and the spiritual covenant of the Lotus Society shall establish a bond from this day forward.
May we all aspire to be born together in the Pure Land, to behold Amitābha together, to transform sentient beings together, and to achieve perfect enlightenment together.
Who then knows that the thirty-two marks and the majestic adornments of a hundred blessings in the future may not originate from this very day?
This begins with the arousal of the bodhicitta and the establishment of vows. May we, together with the great assembly, strive toward this. How fortunate, how fortunate!
*Vow Text for the Nirvana Assembly*:
I respectfully address the Triple Gem of the ten directions, our original teacher Śākyamuni, the compassionate father Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, and Mahāsthāmaprāpta. Nirvana...
All you holy sages gathered here, I pray that out of your compassion you will bear witness to this vow.
I, the bhikṣu [Name], together with the assembly present, have established this assembly and resolved upon the Great Mind for ten reasons. What are these ten?

First, because one reflects on the profound kindness of the Buddha, which is difficult to repay; second, because one reflects on the kindness of one’s parents; third, because one reflects on birth and death...
1. Because of suffering. 2. Because of self-reproach for not having seen the Buddha. 3. Because of observing that the Buddha-dharma is about to perish and sentient beings are pitiable. 4.
Because the *śarīra* relics are difficult to encounter, one rejoices at having encountered them. 5. Because *nirvāṇa* is difficult to meet, one gives rise to a heart of sorrowful attachment.
6. To cause all sentient beings who have not yet planted roots of goodness to plant them; and for those who have already planted them...
To cause roots of goodness to increase; ninth, to cause all sentient beings to take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha, thereby remaining far removed from false views;
tenth, to join with the present great assembly in making vows to seek rebirth in a Pure Land.
Thereupon, before the Buddha, he joined his palms in reverence and made this vow: "First, may my parents of the past..."
Relying on the immediate conditions of this kalpa and through the power of the Triple Gem, may they swiftly leave the evil realms and be born among humans and devas;

by practicing the path gradually, may they all attain Buddhahood. My second vow is that all my unwholesome karma from beginningless time shall be completely extinguished, forever exhausted without remainder.
My third vow is that my afflictions of craving and attachment from beginningless time shall forever...
May they be exhausted without remainder. May I also cause all sentient beings to sever and eliminate all craving. My fourth vow is:
may my affliction of anger from beginningless time be forever exhausted without remainder, and may I also cause all sentient beings to sever and eliminate all anger.
My fifth vow is: may my affliction of false views from beginningless time be forever...
...exhausted without remainder. Furthermore, may I cause all sentient beings to sever and eliminate all false views. My sixth vow is:
may, within my present life, all demonic activities be entirely removed, and may I not undergo any evil retributions whatsoever.
Until I attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), may I, with this physical body of mine, undergo immeasurable suffering on behalf of all sentient beings, causing them to...
May they all attain it; may there be peace and happiness for all. The seventh vow is:

May I swiftly realize the Samādhi of Buddha-remembrance, with mind following upon mind without interval, and thought corresponding to thought, never regressing from the Bodhi of the Buddha. The eighth vow is:
May I attain great wisdom and fully penetrate all Buddha-dharmas. The ninth vow is: May I attain...
Possessing great eloquence, he shall propagate the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, causing immeasurable people to be born in that realm. His tenth vow is:
may he obtain the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining, naturally memorizing all sutras and expounding them for others without weariness.
His eleventh vow is: may he attain the power of great patience and be endowed with the wisdom of great contemplation.
May I not be robbed by fame, reputation, gain, or offerings; may I not be harmed by love, hatred, defamation, or praise;
and may I skillfully transform sentient beings within this world of five turbidities. This is the twelfth vow. As for the thirteenth vow:

May my major and minor precepts, as well as both natural and proscribed offenses, all become pure; may I dwell securely in the holy life and bring sentient beings to maturity. This is the thirteenth vow.
May I, at the time of my death, know in advance that the hour has come; may my body and mind be at ease, and my right mindfulness clear and distinct.
May the holy assembly of Amitābha, holding golden lotus flowers, come to welcome me. In the space of a single thought-moment, may I be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
May all who hear or see this develop faith and all attain the practice to be born in that land. This is the fourteenth vow. May...
My fifteenth great vow is: After I have been born in the Pure Land and attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), I shall return to transform and deliver all sentient beings.
Furthermore, I vow that whenever the Buddhas appear in the world, I may always encounter them, draw near to them, and make offerings to them.
When the Buddha first attained the Way, he was exhorted to turn the wheel of Dharma; when the Buddha entered nirvana, he was entreated to remain long in the world;

and when the Dharma was about to perish, he protected and upheld the True Dharma, causing it to endure for a long time. In places where the Buddha-dharma did not exist, he caused the Buddha-dharma to flourish and manifest, revealing it to all sentient beings.
The sixteenth vow is: "May I, after being born in the Pure Land, swiftly enter the Sahā world.

By means of my supernatural powers and the power of my vows, may the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha be extended until the time of Maitreya’s appearance, so that it shall not be severed. The seventeenth vow is:
I vow that in a future life, I shall extensively expound the Vinaya and establish the True Dharma;
first, I shall gather all sentient beings through the precepts, and subsequently, I shall bring them to fulfillment through meditative concentration and wisdom. The eighteenth vow is:
I vow that in a future life, by virtue of being fully endowed with the power of wisdom and eloquence, I shall utterly destroy all the arguments and discourses of every non-Buddhist (tīrthika). All...
Those with wrong views shall likewise be led to right view. The nineteenth vow is: may I, in a future life, be fully endowed with supernormal powers and the divine eye;

seeing sentient beings who should be subdued, I shall subdue them, and seeing those who should be gathered in, I shall gather them in, causing their roots of goodness to increase and their evil thoughts to be tamed. The twentieth vow is: may I, in a future life, transform and deliver sentient beings.
I know those sentient beings who wish to practice unwholesome dharmas but have not yet succeeded;
I manifest an appearance of evil to terrify them, causing all their unwholesome deeds to fail entirely. My twenty-first vow is:

if there are sentient beings who wish to practice wholesome dharmas but have not yet succeeded, I manifest an appearance of goodness to gladden them, causing all their wholesome deeds to be swiftly accomplished.

The fulfillment of the twenty-second vow: If there are sentient beings who, having committed transgressions, possess a sense of shame and remorse and wish to repent, upon hearing my name, even the ten evil deeds and the five heinous crimes shall all be extinguished without exception.
The twenty-third vow: If there are sentient beings who, while currently performing wholesome deeds, harbor a mind of indolence and wish to fall away from them—
Upon hearing my name, even those who possess but a hair’s breadth of merit shall never again fall back; they shall further diligently cultivate all wholesome dharmas.
My twenty-fourth vow is: may I, in a future age, transform and deliver sentient beings, especially those who are impoverished.

May those who possess hidden treasures be able to enjoy them; may those suffering from illness obtain excellent medicine; may hungry and thirsty sentient beings obtain food and drink; may naked sentient beings obtain clothing;
may sentient beings in distress and calamity be liberated from all sufferings; and may sentient beings who have lost their way [find it].
I shall show them the right path, causing ignorant sentient beings to attain wisdom, and ensuring that all their needs are fulfilled.
I shall cause all sentient beings to first obtain worldly happiness and subsequently attain the unsurpassed supramundane joy of the Dharma.
My twenty-fifth vow is: may I, in a future age during the kalpa of weapons, manifest as a capable general to utterly extinguish the clash of arms.
In an age of pestilence, he manifests as medicinal herbs to cure all manner of ailments; in an age of famine, he manifests as rice and grain;
in places of scorching heat and distress, he manifests as a cooling breeze; in places of parched desolation, he manifests as sweet rain; and in places of peril and obstruction...
Manifesting as a bridge and ferry, he appears as a lamp and torch in places of darkness.

According to the desires of all sentient beings, he manifests whatever they wish to obtain, causing all sentient beings—whether walking or standing, sitting or lying down—to attain peace and happiness.

He resolved to attain bodhicitta. His twenty-sixth vow was: "In a future life, may I protect the Buddha-dharma by manifesting as kings and great ministers in Jambudvīpa, possessing sovereign majesty and power, and transforming and guiding the people so that they practice the Buddha-dharma."
Within his realm, he shall forever sever the karma of killing and refrain from committing evil deeds.
As for those who lack faith and slander the Triple Gem, he shall suppress and subdue them by means of his power. The twenty-seventh vow is:
In future lives, I shall rescue and deliver sentient beings by manifesting as a great makara fish; I shall give my own flesh to sentient beings, which shall be regenerated as soon as it is taken.
It is inexhaustible. Or again, he may manifest as the king of garuḍas, the king of nāgas, the king of horses, the king of oxen, the king of elephants, or the kings of various birds and beasts;
within each of these classes, his majestic virtue and power surpass all others.
He transforms those of his own kind, causing them to abandon the evil realms and resolve upon bodhicitta. The twenty-eighth vow: Should there be sentient beings who are foolish...

They are deluded and lack wisdom. Although they possess faith and devotion, they do not understand the Buddha-dharma. Although they cultivate the path of practice, they do not penetrate the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*).
Although they wish to read and recite, they are unable to retain it in memory. Although they wish to sit in meditation, they cannot eliminate dullness and agitation (*styānamiddha-auddhatya*).
Even when they resolve to perform wholesome deeds, obstacles immediately arise. Or, if they are possessed by evil Māras or wicked companions, I shall, through my supernormal power, cause them—

Their wisdom shall be opened and clarified; they shall thoroughly comprehend the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). All demonic activities (*mārakarman*) shall be entirely distanced from them, and all wholesome dharmas (*kuśaladharma*) shall be swiftly accomplished.

The twenty-ninth vow: Should there be sentient beings who do not possess the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*) and who commit every kind of evil, I shall conceive redoubled compassion for such persons.
Through skillful means (*upāya*), I shall teach and transform them, following after them without abandoning them, even throughout [the course of] kalpas.
For immeasurable kalpas, if this person does not resolve to attain bodhicitta, I shall never abandon them through my compassion and rescue them.

My thirtieth vow is: in a future age, when the Buddha-dharma is about to perish, when malevolent spirits flourish, and when all unwholesome dharmas gather together, I pray that by the power of my great compassion, I shall manifest wherever any evil māras dwell.
He manifests an extremely terrifying form to frighten them; causing their intention to destroy the Dharma, their minds immediately become bewildered and distressed.
When they wish to slander the Dharma with their mouths, their tongues cannot move. When they wish to commit evil with their bodies, their feet cannot be raised.

Their followers are dispersed and scattered, and the evil Māras are extinguished. The thirty-first vow is: for the sake of delivering and saving sentient beings, I enter into the hells to take their place.

They undergo manifold sufferings; may all such painful conditions be gathered upon my own body, so that those sentient beings may give rise to the bodhicitta and be reborn in the celestial realms. My thirty-second vow is:

if there are hungry ghosts for whom fierce fires blaze and who, seeking food and drink, find none, may I, through the power of my great compassion, cause fragrant milk to flow from my hands, and [provide it] to them all.
May they be fully satisfied, with body and mind at peace and bliss, and may they resolve to attain Bodhicitta. The thirty-third vow:

May all animals, who due to their evil karma must endure various sufferings such as being subjected to the blade, the block, and slaughter, have those sufferings taken upon me through my power of great compassion.
Or, may I manifest entry into their midst to cause those who commit killing to repent and cultivate goodness, thereby resolving to attain Bodhicitta.
Bodhicitta. The thirty-fourth vow: There are various hosts of devas who, due to their celestial merit, become arrogant and heedless;
I manifest in a celestial body to admonish them, causing them to awaken to impermanence and swiftly escape the three realms.
The thirty-fifth vow: If there are sentient beings who wish to seek the vehicle of the Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas, I, by means of...
He causes them first to realize the lesser fruits [of the śrāvaka path], whereupon they immediately turn their minds toward the Bodhisattva vehicle. The thirty-sixth vow is as follows:

There may be sentient beings who take pleasure in and are attached to the Lesser Dharma, thereby slandering the Mahāyāna; or there may be sentient beings who cling to the provisional teachings and do not believe in the Perfect and Sudden;
or again, those who, clinging to emptiness, slander existence; or clinging to existence, slander emptiness; or who cling to both emptiness and existence, and thus engage in slander.

Those who slander the Middle Way, and even those who give rise to various divergent views regarding the Buddha-dharma—I shall, by the power of my wisdom and eloquence, refute all such heterodox arguments and extinguish them entirely without remainder.

I shall establish the unsurpassed Buddha-dharma of the One Vehicle, so that all sentient beings may forever be free from doubt within the True Dharma. As for the thirty-seventh vow: when I have finished transforming [sentient beings]...

To deliver sentient beings who practice evil, I manifest in a form identical to their own kind, yet remain untainted by evil dharmas, causing those of similar class to have faith, conviction, and obedience.
Whatever I speak, they all listen and accept; they gradually abandon their evil conduct and cultivate wholesome dharmas.
As for the thirty-eighth vow: in order to transform and deliver various bhikṣus, I manifest various skillful means among the bhikṣus.
Within this assembly, there are those who steal the property of the Triple Gem, violate the precepts by breaking their fasts, hold various wrong views, and do not believe in cause and effect.
Because of these causes and conditions, such persons shall fall into hell.
For their sake, I manifest as the Vajra-holding spirits, the various ghosts and deities, or again manifest the appearances of hell before their eyes, displaying all manner of realms to terrify them.
They shall be struck with fear. They shall cause whatever sins they have already committed to be confessed and repented; they shall not dare to commit again those sins they have not yet committed.
Thus, they shall abandon the causes for rebirth in hell and cultivate supramundane deeds. The thirty-ninth vow is:
"May I further attain immeasurable samādhis, supernormal powers, and wisdom, such that I am fully able to receive and uphold all Buddha-dharmas. The fortieth vow is: "Whatever I..."
I shall dedicate all merits from my cultivation of generosity and observance of the precepts to all sentient beings.
May every single sentient being, having received my gifts, have all their aspirations and requests fully realized, and may they forever abandon whatever they do not desire.
This is the forty-first vow. All the immeasurable difficult practices and ascetic austerities performed by all Bodhisattvas, I...
I shall practice and study all of these until the end of the future, without ever becoming weary or fatigued. The forty-second vow:
All the compassionate vows, merits, and wisdom of every bodhisattva, I shall fully embrace and gather up, leaving nothing behind.
The forty-third vow: May I travel to the worlds of the ten directions to make offerings to all Buddhas with everything...

Flowers of every fragrance, every lamp, every fruit, every food and drink, clothing, banners, pennants, precious parasols, music, song, and dance—all shall surpass those possessed by all the devas. I shall present these to all the Buddhas.
When the Buddhas preach the Dharma for me, I shall listen to and receive it all, without forgetting even a single word or phrase. This is the fourth [vow].
The fourteenth vow is: "May I, in birth after birth and life after life, never forget my original vow, and may I always remain in this land to save sentient beings suffering in distress.
The forty-fifth vow is: "May I be the very first to encounter Maitreya Buddha upon his appearance in the world; having heard the Dharma, may I attain the fruit [of enlightenment].
When that Buddha is on the verge of entering parinirvāṇa, I shall present the final offering. Thus it shall continue until..."
The appearance of Ruci Tathāgata in the world was also like this. As for the forty-sixth vow:

"As long as sentient beings have not been exhausted, the hells have not been emptied, the ocean of karma has not dried up, and the wheel of suffering has not ceased, I shall never vow to first attain the Buddha-way."

The forty-seventh vow: May I, throughout vertical aeons as numerous as atoms and across horizontal worlds as vast as sands, with immeasurable physical actions, immeasurable verbal actions, and immeasurable mental actions, make offerings to all Buddhas and transform and deliver sentient beings.
The forty-eighth vow: When I attain Buddhahood, may my world be so vast that immeasurable Buddha-lands constitute a single Buddha-land. The Buddha...
The body is eternally abiding; the Buddha-dharma is never extinguished. All its realms are most supremely adorned, surpassing all buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Therein, there is neither the True Dharma nor the Semblance Dharma; there are no hells, hungry ghosts, animals, or asuras, nor any māras or their followers.
Although there are devas and humans, they are all great bodhisattvas. That Buddha’s form-body is [inexpressible].
The marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) are inconceivable; the light rays he emits are inconceivable; his retinue is inconceivable;

the sentient beings he transforms are inconceivable. In short, whether as the basis, the correct practice, the master, or the companions, all are inconceivable. If this vow is not fulfilled, I shall never become a Buddha. Thus he resolved.
Having made this vow, he again addressed the assembled multitude with one voice in verse:
"Homage to Śākyamuni, To the true-body relic stupa, To the profound and subtle Dharma,
The Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra, And to all the bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and śrāvaka assemblies."

With a heart of utmost sincerity, I make this true vow: May my former parents and all kinsmen throughout successive kalpas, Both myself and others, together transcend [suffering] and attain rebirth in higher realms;
May we all be liberated, forever severing greed, anger, and ignorance; May we constantly cultivate precepts, concentration, and wisdom, And never give rise to killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct.
May all various wrong views and all evils already arisen be forever extinguished; may those not yet arisen never arise again.

Regarding past evil karmas that would otherwise cause one to undergo the sufferings of hell, may they be repaid a million-fold through the attainment of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
May all demonic obstacles be utterly eliminated within this present life.
Furthermore, by means of the mind that recollects the Buddha, one swiftly realizes the King Samādhi;
with each thought uninterrupted and every moment in accord, one shall never again give rise to regression from unsurpassed Bodhi.
Moreover, may I attain wisdom that penetrates all phenomena and possess unimpeded eloquence.
Proclaiming the gate of mindfulness of the Buddha, One attains the great *dhāraṇī*.
Receiving and upholding all Buddha-dharmas, And further vowing to attain the power of patience (*kṣānti*), One fully cultivates all contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā*).
Tearing asunder the net of hatred and love, Severing the root of fame and profit, The winds at the tops of the trees of praise and blame, Are but traces in the void of beauty and ugliness.
Furthermore, may I be endowed with dignified deportment and attain mastery of the Vinaya-piṭaka;
may all my nature-based and proscribed karmas, both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, be entirely purified. May I bring all sentient beings to fulfillment.
When my life comes to an end, may my mindfulness remain undisturbed as Amitābha and the assembly of sages appear before me.
Extending our hands, we shall hold one another; all who see or hear us shall resolve their minds for enlightenment.
Together we shall be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where we shall behold the Buddha and again hear the Dharma.

Having attained the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), we shall return to this world to transform and deliver all beings, making offerings to the Buddhas and upholding the teachings of all the Buddhas.
When the Dharma of Śākyamuni perishes, by the power of my vows and by the power of my supernormal knowledges,
I shall cause the Dharma to abide long in the world, extending it until the time of Maitreya without interruption.
Furthermore, I vow that in future ages I shall establish the Buddha’s True Dharma and gather sentient beings through the Vinaya.
Later, causing them to attain concentration and wisdom, By the power of great eloquence, He destroys all false views.
Furthermore, with the knowledge of others' minds, He fully knows the hearts of sentient beings;
In both subduing and gathering them, he attains mastery, Causing them to obtain benefit And taming all evil thoughts.
All unwholesome dharmas shall not be accomplished, And wholesome karma shall be swiftly fulfilled.
Those with transgressions who wish to repent, upon hearing this name, are all liberated; When their roots of goodness are about to decline, They are all caused to increase and flourish.
The poor obtain hidden treasures, The sick obtain excellent medicine, And those oppressed by hunger and cold—
May all obtain clothing and food, and may those in distress find liberation.
When the kalpa of weapons arises, may I become a valiant general;
in an age of famine and pestilence, may I transform myself into rice, grain, and various medicinal herbs to universally save all sentient beings.
May I appear as a great king within the realm of Jambudvīpa, transforming sentient beings through the Dharma so that they may sever all karmic acts of killing;
or may I appear as a king of birds or beasts, gathering and transforming those of my own kind—
whether they possess full faith, little faith, or even no faith at all— employing every skillful means for their sake.
Gradually bringing them to subdual, All Māras are made to retreat and disperse;
The hordes are utterly annihilated— From those in hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, Up to the hosts of the various devas— I manifest entry into their midst To cause all to attain liberation.
May the three miserable realms be free from all suffering, And humans and devas transcend the triple world.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna, as well as bodhisattvas of the provisional teachings—
all enter together into the one perfect and sudden [teaching]. For all sentient beings who commit evil deeds,
for the bhikṣus of the Dharma-ending age, and for those with various false views, I, through the power of my skillful means, [will deliver them].
May they give rise to faith and fully penetrate all samādhis;
may the power of the Bodhisattva’s compassion and wisdom, and the power of various merits, cause me to gather all wholesome dharmas in dedication.
May I make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, and may I be fully endowed with every requisite for such offerings.
I and the great assembly, through this shared power of aspiration, shall be companions in every birth, transforming sentient beings everywhere.
Among the three assemblies under the Dragon Flower Tree, may we be the very first to receive the Buddha’s prophecy.
When that Buddha enters parinirvāṇa, I shall provide food and drink; until the realms of sentient beings are exhausted.
There will never be a time when Buddhahood is finally attained; only when all beings have attained Buddhahood shall one then ascend to Perfect Enlightenment.
Dedication Verse (with Preface):

I have heard that for the preliminary guidance of practice, nothing is more supreme than the arousal of the bodhicitta. For the ultimate destination of all virtues, nothing is more essential than dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
This is truly because, from time immemorial, we have been deluded regarding this single mind.

Not knowing that all phenomena are fundamentally empty and that the four great elements do not exist, we vied with one another to cling to views of self and person, giving rise recklessly to hearts of hatred and attachment.

The wholesome dharmas we cultivate are intended only for our own selves, and the merit we acquire is bestowed solely upon our kin; thus, we merely increase the fruits of karma without severing the causes of outflows.
How could one escape the three realms? How could one avoid the four modes of birth? Now, relying upon the teachings, I give rise to the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).
Taking the merits of the past seven days as my immediate basis, and extending to the wholesome dharmas of many lifetimes, I bestow all that is beneficial upon sentient beings.

Abandoning this mind of grasping for existence, I turn toward the true suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Employing this wondrous contemplation of non-arising (*anutpāda*), I seek only...
Aspiring to supreme enlightenment, they knelt with their right knees on the ground and joined their palms, speaking these words:
"Homage to the Honored One of the Three Realms, Śākyamuni Buddha! To the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas of the ten directions and the three periods of time:
We pray only that, through your great compassion, You will together graciously bestow upon us your pity and protection."
Now, relying upon the Buddha’s teaching, I universally arouse the mind of dedication.
Abandoning this mind of conditioned marks, I proceed toward the path of non-arising.
I vow that all the goodness of my three karmas— From beginningless kalpas until this present life— Shall be entirely dedicated for the sake of all sentient beings.
Body and speech are ever pure, and the mind constantly dwells upon wholesome dharmas. May no thoughts of greed or anger arise.
By the power of this repentance, and by the power of these various vows, I entreat the Buddhas to remain long in the world, and further entreat them to turn the wheel of Dharma.
I rejoice in all roots of goodness and bestow them entirely upon all sentient beings.
May all classes of sentient beings have their three obstacles completely eliminated;
may they always see the Buddhas in every birth and constantly hear the Dharma everywhere; may they always give rise to a heart of joy and never harbor thoughts of hatred or envy.
Furthermore, by offering incense to the Buddha, I vow that all sentient beings shall always burn the fragrance of upholding the precepts.
Pervasively perfuming the assembly, he further offers flowers as a tribute, vowing that all sentient beings may have meditative concentration like the blooming of flowers,
so that all who see them are filled with joy. Furthermore, by offering lamps to the Buddha,
he vows that all sentient beings may together kindle the lamp of wisdom, universally illuminating the entire Dharma realm.
By anointing the Buddha-stūpas with incense, may all sentient beings possess patience like that of the ointment, remaining free from hatred and jealousy.
Furthermore, by offering fruit, may all sentient beings fulfill the Buddha-bodhi and together attain the unsurpassed fruit. By giving food as an offering to the Buddhas...
May all sentient beings always partake of the food of Dharma-joy and the food of meditative rapture,
their bodies and minds universally at peace and blissful, filled entirely with joy. By offering this banner to the Buddha,
may all sentient beings overturn greed, anger, and delusion, and together realize the precepts, concentration, and wisdom.
Furthermore, by offering a parasol, may all sentient beings together cover all things with the parasol of unconditioned compassion (*anālambana-maitrī*). Moreover, by offering a victory banner,
may all sentient beings together erect the most supreme banner, rising high above the three realms, and bestow material wealth upon all Buddhas.
May all sentient beings alike possess the seven noble riches, and may the treasury of the Dharma be fully filled.
Furthermore, may I, on behalf of all beings, cultivate and dedicate the Dharma; may the provisional bodhisattvas all return to the gate of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching.
May those of the four fruits of the śrāmaṇya, free from attachment, attain and advance toward supreme wisdom.
May the tainted virtues of humans and devas all become causes for the untainted; may those worldly minds be turned so that they together return to the path of perfect enlightenment.
Deeply understanding the suffering of the three realms, do not give rise to a mind of greedy attachment.
May the hosts of asuras abandon their hearts of pride and arrogance, and [dedicate] all their superior wholesome karma.
Dedicating entirely toward the Buddha-way: the hosts of nāgas, devas, and yakṣas;
the gandharvas, kiṃnaras, and all beings of the eight classes—whatever subtle roots of goodness they possess, whether great or small, all are dedicated toward the Buddha-way.
As for all beings in the human realm, whatever merit they possess, even as slight as a hair’s tip.
Whether in this life or in future lives, I dedicate it all toward the Buddha-way.

When oppressed by the manifold sufferings of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals, if even a single thought of goodness arises, I shall dedicate on their behalf every merit, however minute, so that we may together return to the path of perfect enlightenment. By means of this dedication of merit—
Furthermore, bestowing [merit] upon all sentient beings, universally granting it to all enemies and kin, may they all at once attain the Way of Buddhahood.
One recitation of the Buddha’s name; rinse the mouth for three days. One phrase of Amitābha; all transgressions are extinguished.
The Public Case of the Two Houses: Are they the same or different? If you deliberate and ponder upon them, eighty trillion kalpas will pass.
Chanting the Name of Amitābha is revealed as:
on the upper floor, one chants Amitābha; on the lower floor, Amitābha chants; in the eastern room, the fish-eggs make their sound.
The Buddha’s voice manifests in the western chamber; Whether eating, drinking, dressing, or undressing; Whether spitting, sneezing, defecating, or urinating— Recite the single phrase "Amitābha.
Strike it together into one piece: If you are in the West right now, why wait until the moment of death to see it?
A Verse for Zen Practitioners on the Nianfo (Buddha-Recitation) Case:
"One Phrase of Amitābha" This is a public case (*gong'an*); there is no other deliberation. It is decided directly and immediately:
it is like a great mass of fire—touch it and you are burned; it is like the sword Ta'ao—encounter it and you are mangled.
The eighty-four thousand treasuries of Dharma are fully contained within these six characters;
the seventeen hundred koans are severed with a single stroke.
Let the Buddhas not take pleasure in hearing them; I myself shall remember them heart and mind.
I ask that you need not speak at length; simply maintain single-mindedness and recite the Buddha’s name without distraction.
This serves as an exhortation:
throughout successive lives, it is difficult to escape [suffering], difficult to avoid the cycle of rebirth, difficult to purify one's mindfulness, and difficult to restrain the deluded mind.
Do not practice empty formalities; do not speak of trivial matters. I exhort all people: by no means show this lightly.
This verse for Layman Lü on the Practice of Nianfo:
Nianfo is not a difficult matter; the difficulty lies in single-mindedness. Yet even single-mindedness is not difficult.
The difficulty lies in severing the root of craving; one should contemplate this body.
Its foulness and impurity are beyond full description—whether internal, external, or in between—there is not a single pure thing to be found.
Since one’s own body is thus, so too is the body of another. Generate a deep sense of revulsion and take care never to give rise to attachment.
One should contemplate that the Land of Ultimate Bliss is composed entirely of lotus flowers; there is no reliance on the womb of parents, for one's lifespan is originally immeasurable.
At the very moment one recites the Buddha’s name with a single thought, one is immediately born through transformation within a lotus flower.
If one can maintain this practice without interruption, one will certainly be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).
A Verse for Warning the World:
Within this vast and boundless dream, Who can awaken from the long night? Instead, one clings to the pleasures within the dream;
As awakening approaches, one returns to act again. Yet what is done is not as it was before— One error leads to a hundred errors.
Though you may achieve more than before, you remain as empty and ashamed as ever. Having created karmic deeds within a dream, you pass from suffering into further suffering.
I urge you to turn back your head early; run straight upon the Western Path.
Cast aside all worldly conditions and diligently cultivate pure practices and recitations, looking every day and night for the return home.
With single-minded resolve seeking awakening, The mind-ground suddenly becomes empty;
This is the true Pure Land where Amitābha appears before one— It is originally this very Śākyamuni Tathāgata’s precious stūpa of śarīra.
*Praise of the Precious Stūpa of Śarīra of Śākyamuni Tathāgata*
Our Buddha descended into the world in that Middle Kingdom, manifesting the Eight Great Miracles.
A hundred years later, there arose King Aśoka, who constructed stūpas for the śarīra relics using powdered incense as mortar and the seven precious gems as fine dust.
He employed spirits and deities as laborers, and by the end of the night, they had completed eighty-four thousand stūpas, reaching to the shores of the four seas.
In this land of Zhendan, there are nineteen sites; yet here at Siming alone, sacred traces are but rarely encountered.
During the Western Jin period, when the site was located in Bingzhou, there was a hunter surnamed Liu Shi who entered hell.
The Mahāsattva addressed him, saying: "If you repent, you may seek for śarīra."
Awakening, he left the household life and changed his name to Huìdá. Traveling far from afar to Sīmíng, he sought the Precious Stūpa.

Suddenly, he heard the sound of a bell emerging from the earth; he prostrated himself for seven days until the mountain crags opened of their own accord, and the sacred traces of a thousand years were revealed therein.
Thus, those with the karmic affinity were enabled to behold the Buddha’s body in person.
To this day at Mount Mao, spiritual wonders are extraordinary; people from the four quarters look up in reverence.

Having beheld the signs and beheld the light, I have depicted them and carved them so that they may be transmitted to the four quarters. I compose these words of praise; I bow my head in homage to the Dharma King Amitābha Buddha. Image Praise.
Homage to Amitābha! Who is there that does not know how to recite his name?
