Yet though one recites, if it is not in accord with the practice, mother and child may find it difficult to meet again. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, at all times gather this mind together;
let every thought follow upon the next in continuous succession. When the recitation becomes a single, unified mass, in this way one recites Amitābha.
Amitābha appears spontaneously; one will certainly be reborn in the West. Throughout one's life, there shall be no falling back.
In praise of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara:
The Dharma-body of the Great Being is neither male nor female; since even the body is not a body, upon what else could it rely?
By the power of compassion, a transformation Buddha appears upon the crown of the head; by the power of meditative concentration, the hand holds a wish-fulfilling gem, manifesting majestic virtue.
Mounted upon a wrathful lion, he employs both the methods of subduing and gathering, while simultaneously displaying loving-kindness and patience.
He universally addresses the sons of the Buddha: "You should not grasp at signs; this Bodhisattva is you—neither a painting nor an image."
Furthermore, one should know that self and other are non-dual; to be able to contemplate in this way is the true and inconceivable visualization of the Avalokiteśvara Image.
(Preface) The family of Gu Shanna of Nanguo has long been devoted to the Buddha. On the nineteenth day of the sixth month of the Bingshen year, the Great Being manifested [himself].
An image [of him] was made upon a bamboo screen; his countenance was solemn and majestic. Spectators gathered like a wall around it.

After a while, someone who had treated him with malice suddenly caused the image to vanish. Out of longing and reverence for the virtuous man, people commissioned an artisan to paint his likeness so that they might offer worship to it.
The Great Being manifests his traces, stooping to respond to all living beings: like the moon reflected in a cold pool, or a sound echoed through a hollow valley.
The original enlightenment of sentient beings is none other than Avalokiteśvara; yet, pursuing forms and seeking sounds, they wander through the ocean of suffering.
Taking suffering as the catalyst, one may then attain deliverance; urged by faith and driven toward awakening, I, the Great Being, sport with supernatural powers.
Amidst the curtains and veils, the sacred countenance is solemnly beheld.
The sacred countenance is not small, nor are the curtains and veils large; every fragment is the true body, every mote of dust is the Dharma-realm.
The people of this land are all filled with awe and reverence; they offer incense and flowers, and keep lamps perpetually burning.
They come when conditions arise and depart when conditions end. What is the nature of these responses? It is simply that through sincerity, one attains them.
Thus, they paint images in ink and water to express their offerings, and compose hymns of praise to transmit [the teachings] to the infinite.
Master Yaoshan’s Inscription on Writing in the Void:
Within the vast void, there is absolutely no form or appearance. Lifting the brush to write—what manner of thing is this?
Since the characters leave no trace and the brush is not real, if one turns back to seek the writer, who indeed is that person?
Apart from paper there is no painting; apart from painting there is no paper. Is this paper or this painting? Are they one or two?
Holding up this single principle, he questioned Master Yao. Yao remained serene and did not speak. [This is] "Laughing Until the Void is Shattered," a blood-written eulogy for the image of Mañjuśrī.
You used blood as ink to paint the form of Mañjuśrī;
I took my pen as a tongue to offer praise and worship. Setting down my pen, I ask you:
Which of these is Mañjuśrī—is it the blood, the paper, or is it neither of the two? Thereupon, you bowed your head and replied.
Mañjuśrī, who is not he? Every single stroke is Mañjuśrī. Filling the white paper with horizontal and vertical lines, a transformation Buddha appears within his crown.
Manifesting transformations, he rides upon a lion; at the tip of a single hair, he enters samādhi.
These brushstrokes and ink are no mere play. Alas! You and I—both of us are deluded.
If one encounters the true Mañjuśrī, one should simply smile in silence.
Inscription for the Hall of Pure Practice:
The name of this hall is "Pure Practice. What is its meaning? It is solely purity; it is solely singleness of mind—single-mindedly recollecting Amitābha.
If the mind is not unified, one's karma will be impure; Only through dullness and distraction do afflictions arise. I address you, the assembly:
as you pass through this gate, You should examine yourselves at all times—whether you are diligent or slothful.
If you are slothful, you must rouse your indignation; If you are diligent, you must advance further. Exhausting this single lifetime, you shall surely behold Amitābha.
Inscription for the Inch-Perfume Studio:
When noble guests meet, do not discuss worldly matters. Let the "inch of incense" be our appointment; speak only of the Way. Do not conform to human sentiments;
do not observe conventional etiquette. Whether they understand me or condemn me, let them simply hear it and be done with it.
Inscription for the Hall of the Fast:
Every grain of rice and every stalk of vegetable Is obtained through the generosity of others. If discrimination has not yet been forgotten, A single mouthful is difficult to consume.
Lifting the bowl and raising the chopsticks, One should remember only the Buddha. Only by tasting the true flavor Can one truly repay their virtue.
Eastern Inscription:
Your parents gave birth to you; your teachers and friends perfected you. Now you bear their kindness as a debt, yet you are neither filial nor fraternal.
Your mindfulness of the Buddha is not yet pure, and your deluded mind is not yet restrained. You are hell; hell is you.

The donor of this Western Inscription has built this hall and provided these offerings for you to support your practice of *nien-fo*. You should exert yourself to the utmost and never allow your practice to be interrupted.
It is most forbidden to let other thoughts intermingle with it. Exhort your body and mind; be careful not to be indolent or lax.
When contemplating the sutras and venerating the Buddha, one should certainly honor him; yet the Dharma is even more worthy of understanding. If it were not for the Buddha, who would be our teacher?
If it were not for the Dharma, what could serve as our model? Wherever this sutra resides, there the Buddha resides. Be reverent and cautious; do not be muddled or indolent.
If for a single thought one falters, the myriad demons will swarm; The scattering winds shake the earth, and the murky fog confuses the heavens.
By what means can they be restrained? The power of mindfulness is strong. Only through steadfastness and valor shall this darkness and distraction be subdued.
The source of the mind is originally serene and ultimately pure; When both Buddha and Dharma are forgotten, there is neither medicine nor illness.
Inscription for the Bathhouse:
The four great elements are fundamentally empty; with what, then, shall one wash? The single mind cannot be apprehended; from where could thoughts arise?
If even thought does not exist, how can a Buddha remain? One who can contemplate in this way will surely behold the Compassionate Honored One.
Inscription for the Toilet Chamber:
When performing the great or small excretions, do not forget right mindfulness. The nine orifices flow constantly; this body is loathsome—when shall it be cast aside?
Through the transformation within the lotus womb, in every thought-moment recite Amitābha’s name. The Western Land will surely appear before you.
Inscription for the Bedchamber Those of old repaid their grievances by lying on firewood and tasting gall; Through twenty years of diligent toil, they accomplished their great task.
If life and death are the source of enmity, and the harm received has already been profound, How can one sleep, allowing body and mind to run wild?
The three realms offer no peace; one should not dwell therein for long.
Diligently cultivate right contemplation and seek early escape to the Lotus Buddha-land, where its bliss is vast and overflowing. Return, come back! Do not forget your native land.
— *Preface to the Śarīra Repentance Ritual*
It is said that the Dharma-body has no form, yet it assumes shape through the myriad things; the essence of the Way has no fixed direction, yet it manifests traces in accordance with sentient beings.

Since the Master displayed his passing beneath the twin śāla trees and returned to the source in the middle of the night, the radiance of his jade-like brow has withdrawn from the human world, and the brilliance of his precious countenance has become hidden within the realm.
Of the relics he left behind, three portions were distributed, and thus stupas were constructed in eight kingdoms.
This is the account. This land belongs to the Five Indias; more than a hundred years had passed since [the Buddha's passing] when a holy sovereign appeared, named Aśoka.
He descended upon the world riding an iron wheel and received the Buddha’s prophecy that he would become a king. His will was set upon the field of merit, and his mind dwelt upon the Buddha-dharma.
Upon first hearing of the *śarīra*, he began to seek them. Thereupon, he blocked the "sword-wheel" mechanism of the Gaṅgā River.

It did not turn. He opened King Śibi’s precious casket; the oil and fire were just about to be exhausted. (The *Sūtra of King Aśoka* states: "King Ajātaśatru took the Buddha’s relics and concealed them within the Ganges River.")

He offered a lamp for a thousand years as an act of worship. Within it was placed a golden casket to hold the śarīra, while outside were set revolving wheels of blades that turned on all four sides, driven by flowing water so that the wheels never ceased their motion for even a moment.

When King Aśoka sought to take them, he could hardly manage to do so. There was a bhikṣu named Padma who instructed him to throw a pomegranate at them; the wheels then stopped turning, and he was able to retrieve the śarīra. As soon as the golden casket was opened, the oil was exhausted and the fire was extinguished.

Thus, employing the intellectual power of spirits and deities, and seeking the supernatural powers of an arhat, he gathered various fragrances to form clay and ground the seven precious gems into powder.
The eighty-four thousand Buddhist stupas were completed during the middle watch of the night. Within the realm of three thousand three hundred people, they were immediately distributed.

A hundred deities exerted their feet, vying to race toward the light of his five fingers; ten thousand ghosts raised their heads, all beholding his arm extending halfway into the sky. (Yuzhuan Wangzhi says:

King Ashoka took the Buddha’s relics and commanded various spirits and deities to use fragrant mud and the seven precious gems to construct eighty-four thousand stupas in a single night. He then invited the Venerable Kshapanaka to extend his fingers and emit light.)

There are eighty-four thousand paths. Each of the spirits followed one ray of light to its end and placed a finger there. The Venerable One, in mid-air, shielded the sun with his hand; as the spirits looked toward it, throughout the heavens, the stūpas [were completed] within a single day.
At the same time, stupas were established, and thus their veneration began to flourish; the Buddha-dharma consequently prospered greatly.

While those [stupas] located in Central China numbered in the many thousands, these belonging to the East numbered only nineteen. The year King Aśoka constructed his stupas was the era of the joint regency (*gonghe*) of King Li of Zhou.
In other locations, sacred traces are rarely preserved; it is only here at the Four Mountains that such numinous vestiges remain.
This matter remains significant. Formerly, during the Taikang era of the Western Jin dynasty, there was one Liu Sahuo of Bingzhou, who was the Bodhisattva Ribin.
Out of compassion for sentient beings creating karma, he manifested in a form similar to them to transform people; having incurred offenses, he entered the dark realms of the underworld.

Fearing suffering, he sought deliverance. A foreign monk directed him, saying, "Seek the *śarīra* (relics). Upon awakening, he resolved his mind [on enlightenment] and immediately changed his occupation.
Having left his secular life to respond to the world, he temporarily served as a hunter; yet when the Great Being renounced the world, he returned to the appearance of a *bhikṣu*.
Thereupon, turning his back on Bingfen in the north, he traveled south through Jiangzhe. He gazed longingly toward the *buddha* (the stupa), mindful of the *śarīra*.
Driven by this pursuit, how could he have feared the hardships of galloping across ten thousand li of passes and mountains?
How could he have known the toil of traversing roads for several years? Thus, he ascended Mount Mao and wandered upon Jade Terrace.
Suddenly, the resonance of bells was heard from beneath the earth, and a stupa rose high atop the crags. A single expanse of green mountain revealed the sacred traces of a millennium; several...
Upon these heavy, solid rocks, the divine traces of ten thousand ages shall remain forever. From this time forth, pagodas were erected and monks ordained;
relying upon the monks to guard the pagodas, the land was hailed as the Buddha-land of the Southeast, and its monks were celebrated as dragon-men for generations.

When the auspicious destiny of the Liang dynasty began, the title of this mountain was finally revealed; when the Great House first rose to prominence, the inscriptions of its temple were resplendently renewed, and auspicious omens appeared repeatedly.
Miraculous wonders occurred in succession. Sometimes auspicious marks and features would manifest within a stupa; sometimes radiant light would be emitted from the tops of pine trees.

By prostrating for several weeks, a compassionate parent was freed from the calamities of karmic retribution in the dark realms. By practicing cultivation for several months, a venerable master obtained the auspicious omen of a seal-mark.
Even some offered a single arm, their spirit returning to the Pure Land of the Nine Lotuses; others sacrificed their entire bodies, personally realizing [enlightenment].
Regarding the Samādhi of Buddha-Recollection: Shi Xian laments his own late birth, whereby he was unable to behold the Buddha’s physical body in person.

Yet, fortunate as he is that his karmic conditions are profound, he has still been able to encounter the sacred traces of the Sage in person. In the summer of the year Jihai, he specifically offered prostrations and paid homage;

he respectfully visited this mountain, observing the three-month retreat and repenting at the six periods of the day. However, because his ordinary sincerity is shallow and inferior, it is difficult to move the Compassionate One; his past karma is deep and heavy.

Having failed to receive a response through such signs, I have therefore restated the ritual procedures and renewed my most earnest supplications. I shall devote my entire life to this practice, making it the limit of my existence.

Not only do I examine my own transgressions, but I also join others in repentance. Like one suffering from a chronic illness who has not yet recovered, I feel constant compassion for those with the same ailment;
like a wayward son who has not returned home, I frequently shed tears of longing for my kin. These words are not worthy of being regarded as a literary masterpiece, yet their meaning may perhaps...
This may be adopted. It is hoped that the mountains of hindrances will be overturned and transformed into mountains of merit; that the ocean of karma will dry up and become an ocean of wisdom;

Regarding the "Brief Account of the Nirvana Assembly":

I have previously read the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. When the Buddha was approaching his nirvana, humans and devas presented offerings, and the great assembly was filled with sorrow; their entire bodies were covered in blood.
It is as if one were looking at a *pāri-jātaka* flower. There are those who, unable to bear seeing the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa, first attained extinction themselves.
Alas! How profound was their sorrow and longing, reaching such an extreme. Now that we are far removed from the sun of the Buddha, we dwell in the age of the Final Dharma (*mappō*).
The assembly of those who have left the household life, on the day of the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, did not know to present offerings, nor did they feel any sorrow;
furthermore, they were unaware that this day was the anniversary of the Buddha’s passing into extinction. Alas! As disciples of the Buddha, how could it be appropriate to act in such a manner?
Indeed, the day of the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa* is like the anniversary of one’s parents’ death. For a person to be a child yet remain ignorant of their parent’s memorial day—how can this be?
Is this what is meant by filial piety? To fail to contemplate the performance of ancestral sacrifices on such a day—can this be called reverence?
Although there are differences between the mundane world and the supramundane, the way one brings forth a heart of filial and reverent devotion is one and the same.

Indeed, while parents of the mundane world give birth to our physical bodies and nourish our lives, and though their kindness is profound, it eventually comes to an end; yet even such parental affection...
Worldly parents are partial; though they toil, they also rest. The supramundane parents are not like this: they give birth to my Dharma-body and nourish my life of wisdom.
They push me toward the dryness of the realms of humans and devas and remove me from the dampness of the three miserable paths.
They swallow for me the bitterness of impermanence and spit out for me the sweetness of permanence. They feed me with concentration and wisdom.
She nourished me with her milk and covered me with the garment of shame and remorse. She sustained and protected me with total devotion;
day and night, she diligently nurtured her child without ceasing for immeasurable kalpas, never considering the toil or hardship.
She knew only the thought of loving her child and disregarded all else. When he was young, she worried that he might fall away; and when he reached maturity...
He stands there, moreover grieving over their premature death; thus his compassion and loving concern for them never cease.
Furthermore, he does not feel love for virtuous sons nor hatred for wicked sons; his mind is always impartial, protecting all without bias.
Yet, because his children were foolish and mistakenly took poison, the compassionate father devised a skillful means: he left the medicine behind and went away.
A messenger was sent back to announce that your father had already died, yet in truth he did not die. What is the poison? It is called affliction (*kleśa*).
What is the medicine? It is called the Buddha-dharma. What is the expedient means (*upāya*)? It is called *nirvāṇa*. What is the messenger who was sent?
It is called the *śarīra* relics. You should know that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for us, thus manifested these through expedient means.
He has entered nirvana, yet in truth he has not passed into extinction. The Buddha possesses such benevolent virtue toward sentient beings, yet all beings remain in profound ignorance;
is this not a cause for sorrow? As for the relics of the Tathāgata, although there are nineteen locations within the land of Zhendan (China), sacred traces are rarely preserved;
only at one place, Maofeng, do they still exist to this day, their spiritual wonders beyond measure.

First: Is it not the case that the people of Siming (Four Illuminations) have planted roots of goodness in past lives, such that they are able to behold the deeds of the Tathāgata’s manifested transformation during this final age?
Although the Dharma-body of all Buddhas pervades all places, the methods by which the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) gathers and transforms beings do indeed have their specific modes.
Where the śarīra is located, there the Buddha is present. Therefore, one should know that even though we dwell in the final age, if one possesses faith, [the Buddha is present].
We have long been blessed by the compassionate countenance of our Teacher. Even though a Buddha has appeared in the world, if we lack faith, it is no different from never having seen him at all.
This is precisely why we must exert ourselves with diligent effort, giving rise to the thought that such an encounter is difficult to find and a cause for great rejoicing.

Indeed, our spiritual faculties are inferior and our merit is meager while our defilements are heavy; thus, we have not attained the vision of the Truths within this present life. Now, together with this assembly, we establish [this vow].
This assembly is convened once every year, with a lifetime as its term. One performs seven days of prostrations and repentance, and offers food and drink of a hundred flavors;
this may be called the final offering, truly expressing the sincerity of one’s longing and devotion. Whatever merit is thereby produced—

It is not for my own benefit, but to bestow [merit] universally upon all sentient beings. I seek neither the realms of humans nor devas, but only aspire to the Pure Land, so that it may serve as a causal condition for my future liberation and provide the means for rebirth and seeing the Buddha, thereby repaying the Buddha’s kindness even in the slightest degree.
Yet, there are those who begin with vigor but fail at the end; this is what the sages have cautioned against. It is the common human nature to be diligent at first and indolent later.
Without binding oneself with vows, how can one ensure permanence? Without taking the *yati* (the restrictive rules) as the standard, how can one restrain body and mind?

Therefore, having deliberated upon what is appropriate for the occasion, we have established these regulations and announced them to the great assembly. Should any matter arise that requires an exception, it shall be dealt with accordingly.
Proceed. May we together preserve and uphold this. Should it prove otherwise, I would be grateful for your instruction. (The regulations are recorded separately following the *Nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī*).

Second Preface to the *Nirvāṇa Assembly Regulations*: I have been a renunciant since childhood. Whenever I was among the great assembly of monks, I would address the elders, saying: "The Tathāgata has entered *nirvāṇa*..."
When did this occur? The assembly was unable to respond. Some offered explanations, yet their arguments were inconsistent and lacked foundation; I harbored doubts within my heart.
Furthermore, I frequently observed monks and laypeople preparing vegetarian feasts for the Buddha, most of which were not in accordance with the Dharma.

They often displayed on the sacrificial tables foods that people find unpalatable, claiming these as offerings. This not only yields no merit, but moreover incurs the fault of showing disrespect to the Buddha.
I have always been filled with deep regret. Upon reaching maturity, I traveled to various lecture halls and examined the texts of the Tripiṭaka.

While reading the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* in my leisure time, I first learned that on the fifteenth day of the second month, at the rising of the sun, the Tathāgata emitted light to assemble the multitude and declared, "Today I shall enter parinirvāṇa.
The great assembly, having received this light, gathered together all at once. At that very moment, offerings were presented...
Clouds gathered as he shed tears like rain; banners and streamers reached the heavens; and sacrificial offerings were spread across the earth.
Every one of the six flavors of this world was present, and every one of the five sensory objects of the heavens was provided to the utmost—nothing was lacking. Alas! How magnificent it was!

Furthermore, I once read the *Lizanwen* (Text on Prostrations and Praises) by Dharma Master Jingjue, wherein I saw his verses praising the appearance of the Tathāgata’s nirvana, describing it in successive detail.

As if it were before my very eyes, I felt the utmost sense of longing and devotion; thus I knew that there were ancients whose hearts were the same as mine, though in recent times such practices have been rare.

In the spring of the Jihai year, I crossed the river from Xiling and reverently visited Mount Ayuwang in Siming to pay homage to the true-body relics of Śākyamuni Tathāgata, whereupon I immediately received the full precepts at that very site.
At the Xia Temple, once the summer retreat (*an-gu*) had concluded, he burned a finger as an offering to the Buddha; yet his heart remained unsatisfied.

Flowers. In the spring of the following year, he returned once more to this mountain. On the anniversary of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa, he gathered several disciples and first established this assembly.

It was not cold; the offerings required were rare and extraordinary, neither cheap nor coarse. Among these, on the first day, he made offerings to the Buddha according to the liturgical texts for praise.

On the second day, he performed the rite of repentance (*li-ch'an*), following his own composed ritual manual. This continued until the seventh day, when the rites of repentance were concluded and ended with the dedication of merit through mindfulness of the Buddha (*nianfo huixiang*).
The assembly all sighed in wonder, saying, "This is unprecedented! Shaming is a most excellent place in the world."
It benefits my Buddha’s true body. Now that spiritual friends from the four directions have gathered together at once, this excellent undertaking has been accomplished;
it is no small matter, and it must not be left unfinished. From now on, this shall be performed once every year, with the remainder of one's life as the term.
This is a duty that must necessarily be fulfilled within the lot of a Buddha’s disciple; it cannot be treated like ordinary matters.
The observance of the ritual for repentance and the recitation of sutras while receiving offerings are discussed here as being of the same day. I told the assembly:

"There are three difficult matters regarding this assembly. For instance, in seeking śarīra relics, although there are nineteen locations within the land of China, the years and months have long passed."
The holy sites have mostly fallen into ruin; only one location, Moshan (鄮陰), remains extant to this day. To have the good fortune to behold it after countless kalpas is the first rarity.
More than two thousand years have passed since the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa; while making offerings at the site of his nirvana existed in antiquity, [to do so now is rare].

Nowadays, such things are rarely heard of. That we have been pursued by our past karmic affinities to meet here from a thousand li away, gathering from all quarters to practice together for seven days—within this world, is this not truly rare?
This is the second difficulty. In various regions, societies are formed to establish periods of practice;
they exist everywhere. Yet, among the disciples of the Buddha, one hears only of receiving wealth through ritual repentance, but never of giving away wealth.
When performing rites of repentance, before the thought of the Way has arisen, the mind for personal gain already emerges.

Now it is not so; sincerity and reverence issue from within the heart, while wealth and goods are relinquished beyond the body. In my shame and urgency, I dare not weary of toil. Though I have not yet repaid [your kindness], I truly harbor deep longing and devotion.
Such thoughts as these—none but the Buddha knows them. This was the third difficulty. Before he had finished speaking, a challenge arose from the side.
One said: "I have heard that the Dharmakāya of the Buddhas pervades all places; fundamentally, there is neither emergence into the world nor parinirvāṇa.
Since there is no parinirvāṇa, how can there be a memorial day? As for the school of the Chan lineage, it upholds the direct command alone;
since even Buddhas and patriarchs are not established therein, how could there be such things as sweeping stupas or making offerings? Now, regarding this non-arising..."
Within the state of cessation, you falsely perceive arising and ceasing. You prepare a hundred flavors of delicacies to provide for it, and assemble the fourfold assembly to pay it homage.
Furthermore, you do not offer respectful ceremonies at the hermitage where it resides, but must travel far to Mount Mao specifically to venerate the śarīra.

Is this not to abandon what is near to seek what is distant, to be attached to external objects while losing sight of the mind, and to fail to comprehend the nature of reality? I said: "What you have said..."
"This is the principle. Now I shall question you on certain matters; may you answer them with truth? He replied, 'I may.
[The Master] then questioned him, saying, 'Do you have both parents living? He said, 'In my youth I was unfortunate; they passed away early, and for a long time I have been deprived of their care.
[The Master] said, 'When your parents have passed away, has their spirit also perished? He said, 'Their spirit has never perished.'"
Question: Does the spirit have a fixed location? Answer: Since the spirit is formless, how could it have a fixed location? Question:

In that case, when performing sacrifices at the prescribed times, do you still go to your parents' graves? Answer: Although I am unfilial, regarding these ritual observances, I still dare not neglect them.
I said: "I was in error. If your parents are present as spirits, then [the sacrifice] has never been absent."
Once dead, they have never truly died; yet to offer sacrifices to them is to extinguish their spirit. To sacrifice to an extinguished spirit—who is there to receive the offering?

Furthermore, since spirits have no form and no fixed location, they are not confined within a tomb. A single thought of utmost sincerity is surely sufficient to reach them through spiritual resonance.
Why, then, must one leave one’s home and family, travel far to a grave or shrine, and labor wearily upon the road?
"Shall we establish the practice of traveling back and forth by boat and carriage for the purpose of performing ancestral sacrifices and sweeping the graves? He replied:
"Although we know that the spirits of our parents exist while their physical bodies no longer remain, we therefore offer to their spirits. Though the spirits do not eat, it is as if they did.

Is this not similar to obtaining food in a dream, where one’s hunger or satiety is perfectly real? Although the spirit has no fixed location, it must necessarily have something upon which it relies; therefore—"
To provide them with burial mounds so that they may be offered sacrifices and swept clean is the means by which one consoles the spirits of the deceased and fulfills the way of the living.
I said: "If you understand this, then what you find difficult to comprehend will be resolved. Have you not reflected upon it?
You know that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, yet you do not know that its manifested traces pass away; you know that the Dharma-nature is all-pervasive, yet you do not know..."
If there were no traces of response (nirmāṇakāya), how could the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) be manifested? If there were no śarīra relics, who would know of the traces of response?

Since it is said that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, how could there be any separation from the response-body? Since it is said that the essence of the Dharma is all-pervading, how could it be restricted solely to the śarīra?

You wish to cast aside phenomena to seek the principle and discard existence to discourse on emptiness; yet you remain deluded regarding phenomenal characteristics—how much more so regarding the ultimate penetration!

Is this not rational? Formerly, when Mahākāśyapa was about to enter Mount Kukkuṭapāda to await Maitreya Buddha, he vowed that he would first travel to the heavens and the dragon palaces, as well as throughout the world, to pay homage to all the stupas before entering meditative absorption. Now, Mahākāśyapa was the patriarchal founder of the Dharma-gate;
how could it be that he did not understand the nature of reality (dharmatā) and acted thus? One should know that the Nirvāṇa of the Tathāgata is [not something that can be reached by such means].
It is inconceivable. It is neither eternal nor annihilated; it is free from existence and free from non-existence. One should not give rise to conceptual discrimination through biased views.
Because you maintain that the Dharma-body is eternally abiding, you have failed to comprehend the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) in benefiting sentient beings.
This is truly due to your failure to deeply clarify the principles of the teachings. As stated in the Sūtra: "It is like an infant."
"The mother was always by his side, yet he did not conceive the thought that she was difficult to encounter. When the mother was about to depart, he immediately felt a heart of longing and yearning.
The Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa is, in essence, like this. Do you, my son, understand this? Someone said: "What you have said is correct.
However, I have heard Confucius say: 'Even two grain-offering vessels may be used for a sacrifice. The *yue* sacrifice is superior."

Regarding the killing of an ox, what is the point of taking a hundred flavors? [The interlocutor] says: "The words of Confucius likely emphasize that manifesting illustrious virtue is paramount, rather than regarding elaborate sacrifices as honorable;
they do not mean that one must be fixed upon using only two bamboo baskets. For instance, when praising the filial piety of King Wu and the Duke of Zhou, it is said:
"In spring and autumn, they repaired their ancestral temples, displayed their ancestral vessels, set out their ceremonial robes, and presented seasonal offerings."
Regarding "timely food," it means that for each of the four periods of the day there are specific items; thus, it is clear that two sacrificial vessels (*duī*) are not intended here.
Furthermore, regarding the praise of Great Yu, it says: "He used coarse food yet offered filial piety to the spirits.

Observing these words concerning filial piety, one can further understand that while his own sustenance was frugal, his offerings to the deities were necessarily abundant. As for a Bodhisattva making offerings to the Buddha, they exhaust the resources of the world.
Even such sweetness would not be considered much; how much less so these meager hundred flavors! Others may further say:
"Among all forms of offering, the offering of the Dharma is supreme. Now, my son does not practice the offering of the Dharma, but instead devotes himself exclusively to conditioned things.
"Is this not the application of the Bodhisattva’s mind? The Master said: "You have again misunderstood the essential meaning of the sutra.

The intent of the sutra is that these offerings of incense and flowers each flow forth from the great compassion and great vows of the Bodhisattva, and are accomplished through great practice and great power.
This is essentially discussing the Dharma through material things; because phenomena and principle are perfectly integrated, it is called a 'Dharma-offering. It is as follows:"
According to your interpretation, the various adornments and offerings of Samantabhadra would all be conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), which would constitute self-destruction;
how could this possibly be the intent of the sutras? You should know that while veneration of the Buddha primarily concerns the inner mind, it also encompasses external objects.

If one possesses the intention but lacks the power [to provide], then even a light object becomes heavy [in merit]. Conversely, if one has the power but lacks the intention, then even a heavy object [is rendered ineffective].
Yet this is still considered light. Between having strength but lacking intention and having intention but lacking strength, it is better to value having the intention despite lacking the strength.

Only when both mind and strength are fully exerted, and internal and external factors mutually support one another, will affairs and principles be harmoniously integrated; only then is success achieved. Now, however, there is no sincerity or reverence within.

Externally, they are again stingy with wealth, yet they speak recklessly of "Mind-Only. Where, then, is this mind? Generally speaking, the sentiments of people in these degenerate times value the secular and despise the true;
they honor men and slight the Buddha. When entertaining guests, they provide an abundance of fine delicacies; when making offerings to the sages and worthies, they present only meager, coarse food.
As for their own sustenance, they select the fattest and freshest meats every morning; yet as for serving the Buddha, they do not maintain such devotion even for a single day.

Regarding "sweet and delicious": if one speaks of fragrance, it refers solely to the incense of the mind; there is no need for *suhaka* resin. If one speaks of fruit, it honors only the fruit of the Path;

how could one value the *āmra* fruit? The offering of the Dharma is supreme; why must one rely on worldly wealth? One sustains oneself through the joy of meditation (*dhyāna-prīti*); what need is there for solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*)?

Their stinginess is firmly sealed; they borrow the words of the Buddha to gloss over their vulgar sentiments. With meager cultivation of the seeds of goodness, they plant the banner of pride and increase the thorns of dogmatic views.
Furthermore, when they see a person of high status, they scurry about to welcome and flatter them; yet when facing a Buddha image, they lean back or lie down and refuse to rise.
Upon hearing the Dharma for a short while, one immediately falls into lethargy; yet when engaging in intense conversation all day long, there is never any weariness or fatigue.
Amidst the bustle of various worldly affairs and diversions, one always finds plenty of time; yet when offering incense to the Buddha, even for a brief moment, there is not the slightest leisure.

When it comes to seeking fame or pursuing profit, they travel the roads for years on end without wearying of the journey; yet when it comes to performing rituals, repentance, or reciting sutras, they enter the altar hall for but a moment and immediately feel exhausted.
As soon as they begin to recite the Buddha’s name, they say their mouths are sour; when they just happen to bow in prostration, they claim their backs ache.
These are all the universal ailments of the world, which we ought to contemplate deeply and guard against with earnest remorse.
I am unworthy and have been unable to emulate the ancients in upholding this Way; I am a transgressor against the Dharma-gate, for whom there is no escape from blame.
Now, I have established this assembly, desiring in secret to repay the Buddha’s kindness above and rescue the obscurations of the age below; yet my status is humble and my virtue meager.
"I was unaware that what I said was untenable. May you, sir, not reject my words because of who I am; I beg you to examine them with favor.

From this day forward, I shall not dare to debate this again. He bowed twice more with his head to the ground and said, "Since you have so excellently established the beginning, you should now plan for the conclusion."
To ensure a good end, if there are no established rules and regulations, how can these practices endure for a long time?

Therefore, in response to the request of my fellow members of the society, I have briefly set forth the following articles. I have also arranged their discourse in sequence and placed it at the beginning of this manuscript to inform those who come after.

The Bhikṣu Śikhin respectfully presents this offering of incense and candles, praying to the Spirit Eel Bodhisattva who protects the stupa at the Golden Sand Well on Mount Aśoka: "I have heard that the Great..."

Consequently, the former court issued an imperial edict proclaiming his honored title and ordering that...
The officer in charge of the year’s harvest slaughters a pig to present as a sacrifice, in order to repay [the Buddha's] meritorious grace.
The Bhikṣu Xian has now come to this mountain and prostrated before the Buddha’s stūpa on two occasions. He personally witnessed the act of slaughter;

the sounds of lamentation pierced his ears, almost beyond his power to bear, and the grief cut into his heart so deeply that he could not restrain himself. Therefore, he cast this letter into the depths of the pool, offering a piteous appeal to the Great Being. Great...
The Great Being protects and upholds the Buddha-Dharma; he saves the world and brings peace to the people. His merit is vast, and his benefit is profound.
To have the officials slaughter [the animal], though it be by the command of the state, is not the heart of a Great Being. Yet, as for that which is created by karma, there must surely be its cause;
as for where retribution falls, how could it be without its recipient? If it does not fall upon the Great Being, where else would it go? Since the Great Being has already...

To protect the Buddha-Dharma, one must embody the Buddha-mind. This Buddha-mind is none other than sentient beings themselves; apart from sentient beings there is no Buddha, and apart from the Buddha there are no sentient beings.
How can you allow future Buddhas to suffer affliction for a long time without considering how to rescue them?
Furthermore, while the supernatural powers of a Great Being can eliminate thirst among an entire army, they cannot exempt one from the pain of suffering.
If a single pig can bestow sweet rain upon the world, why cannot it preserve the lives of sentient beings?
How fortunate are humans to receive such protection, yet what crime has the pig committed that it is not spared?
Is it perhaps because of its attachment to its own palate that it entrusts itself to the butcher’s hands to receive fragrant flavors? For even a Great Being does not cherish his own body.
How much less could one crave the flesh and blood of sentient beings? Now that you wish to bring peace and happiness to sentient beings, how could you instead inflict upon them slaughter and harm?
I am a disciple of the Buddha’s bequeathed teachings; upholding the Buddha’s prohibitions, I ought to proclaim the Buddha’s words to others.
If I do not speak of this, who else could? Now, for the sake of the Great Being, I shall set forth his transgressions, which are briefly tenfold.
Only a divine being can discern this. Now, for a Mahāsattva to deliver sentient beings, compassion is the foundation.
If one lacks this mind, they are not a Bodhisattva. Since a Mahāsattva is called a Bodhisattva, how can they fail to cease killing?
To not cease killing is to lack a compassionate heart; this is the first fault. A Mahāsattva regards others as themselves and regards all things as they do humans. Even now, though...
If one’s assistance to others does not even equal that given to material objects, this violates the mind of equanimity; this is the second fault.

Having become a disciple of the Buddha, how could one fail to uphold the Buddha’s precepts? Even if one has not formally received the five precepts, the precept against killing must be maintained. If a Mahāsattva does not maintain it, he is at fault.

one’s own Buddha must still be revealed by another Buddha. Since the direct cause (正因) must rely upon the revealing cause (了因) for illumination, for what reason do you so earnestly and painfully exhort us?
It is solely because this Sahā world is a pit of fire.
After awakening, do not say that you have no need to see the Buddha; you should know that after awakening, one truly seeks rebirth [in the Pure Land]. (Tianru said:

"If you awaken to the mind, then rebirth in the Pure Land cannot be turned back even by ten thousand oxen. Those who are still ignorant must not abandon their teachers to study; young children should still walk close to their mothers. After the Elder Zhe...

Once the body has rested, do not tread upon it again. (Song Zhe-lao resided at a great monastery in the capital for forty years without sleeping; he practiced seated meditation with such intense austerity that after his death in a sitting posture, śarīra were produced when his paper robes were cremated.

He was subsequently reborn in a place of great wealth and nobility, yet throughout his life he suffered much grief and pain. The overturned carriage of Master Qing—how could its tracks be followed? (Master Song Qing-Cang’s subsequent incarnation became Duke Zeng).
One must personally realize the state beyond birth before returning to the Sahā world to deliver sentient beings.
I ask: what strategy is there for rebirth? One must rely upon the complete integration of faith, practice, and vows. First plant the root of faith within the field of the mind;
once practice is sufficient, further strengthen it with the power of vows. Without provisions for the journey, one will never arrive (if there is faith and vows but no practice);

without a bridle to guide the horse, who can move forward (if there is faith and practice but no vows)? Simply take these three matters as a seal of agreement, and join hands to ascend together to the nine grades.

Appreciate the lotus; do not disdain the abundance of delusive thoughts when recollecting the Buddha. Try to observe from where these delusive thoughts arise. To try to gather and restrain them mindlessly is surely a sickness;

to intentionally seek to dispel them is likewise a demon. It is like trying to extinguish a fire by embracing firewood—it only adds to the blazing flames; it is like digging a breach in a dyke to let out water—it only causes a flood.
In the long river [of dharma], you must recite each word with perfect clarity. When recitation reaches its limit and the mind is forgotten, what remains?
The sound of the Buddha easily dispels dullness and distraction; as it leaves the mouth, it returns to the ear.

Suddenly, the tangled weeds are consumed by fire, and the sky-obscuring thick mist is dispersed by the wind. With one's entire being being the Buddha, who is there to recite? A lotus blooms throughout the entire world.

If you plant [the seeds] now, why wait until the end of life to be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Right now, sitting upright upon the jade pavilion, the four characters of "Amitābha" are beyond all deliberation;
it is simply a matter of holding them single-mindedly without momentary forgetfulness. If you weary of the ordinary, you will ultimately be cut off from it;

as soon as you seek the profound and mysterious, you fall into deviation. One may taste the olive roughly and know nothing of its flavor, but only by chewing the salted vegetables finely does one finally perceive it.
Perceiving the fragrance, one’s mindfulness reaches the state where body and mind are empty and still; there is no need to open one's mouth to ask about the Western Land.

Reciting the name of Amitābha Buddha requires single-minded dedication. When the practice deepens, mindfulness becomes naturally pure. With every thought, the essence of the true nature is perfectly luminous; with every sound, the original person is awakened.
Like an infant who has fallen into water and repeatedly calls for its mother, or a wayward son who finally returns home—only then does he truly recognize her.
Seeing their kin, they speak again of past partings; this only causes them to sob until tears soak their kerchiefs.

If you wish for your practice to be uninterrupted, you must apply yourself with diligence for it to truly correspond to the Way. To lose mindfulness for even a moment is like clouds obscuring the sun;

to give rise to a single thought for a flash is like a moth covering a lamp. A small stream flowing long enough will eventually pierce stone; boiling water, if the fire is extinguished, will likewise cool.
The formation of ice; rebirth as a Buddha is but a trivial matter. It depends entirely upon the power of one’s own mindfulness.
If you wish to know the definitive point of mindfulness of the Buddha, within this there is no reckoning of progress or stages. When dust settles, the ancient mirror shines ever more brightly;
when the wind ceases, the cold pond’s water naturally becomes still. The four natures are originally empty and the mind is vividly clear; the three bodies cannot be grasped—this is the Buddha.
Brilliantly clear! This single gate fully encompasses all skillful means; cessation and contemplation are not achieved through gradual stages.
While walking, one should maintain right mindfulness of Amitābha; with every step, one follows a Buddha across. Beneath one’s feet, one constantly roams the Pure Land;
in every thought within the heart, one severs ties to Saṃsāra. When passing by flowers or willows, there is no need to look back; when facing water or ascending a mountain, do not—
Let him go. When I am reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, I shall come and go through the ten directions as I please.
While dwelling here, it is well to practice mindfulness of the Buddha and contemplate the body: which among the four elements is the true self? I and Amitābha are not two;
like a shadow joined with the bright moon, we are exactly three. This empty room is gradually decaying and will be hard to inhabit; when the rotten beams are about to collapse, how can one remain?

How easy it is to sit upright! When shall I be like a cicada newly emerged from its shell? My spirit dwells alone within the womb of the lotus; when seated, I gaze upon the Buddha’s feet in the full-lotus posture.
My body rests upon the lotus pedestal as the flower blooms fully; the marks of the white tuft appear clearly according to my thoughts, and the golden countenance manifests in harmony with my mind.
All phenomena are like dreams and illusions, fundamentally empty and still; when the principle reaches perfect integration, it is beyond [duality].
Existence and non-existence. On what day at the edge of the pond did you cup his two feet, personally receiving the pouring of the *amṛta* upon your crown?
When lying down, recite the Buddha’s name without opening your voice; within your breath, skillfully bind His name.

With a single pillow of clear breeze across ten thousand miles of autumn, and half a bed of bright moonlight through the third watch of night—there is no further worldly entanglement for the mind to sever; there is only the dream of the lotus flower.
It is easily accomplished. When the eyes are blurred by sleep, the Buddhas appear; upon awakening, the memory remains vivid.
Monks should practice mindfulness of the Buddha with diligent effort, so as to attain the pure karmic conditions for the Lotus Pond. Hearing the Dharma in person is more than merely facing the text;
one suddenly clarifies the mind without the need for Chan meditation. How could a wise teacher surpass Amitābha? Among virtuous friends, who dwells in the realm of Sukhāvatī?
Standing before [the Buddha], in a single thought-moment, one travels throughout all Buddha-lands. (Monks,) do not mock those who travel the mountains and rivers in weary pilgrimage;
this very place is where the True Teaching resides within the Confucian tradition. If you merely exhaust your present form, future lives will be empty.

Though practicing benevolence and righteousness with earnest sincerity, as soon as one speaks of birth and death, it becomes obscure and hazy. You should seek the path home and contemplate the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*); do not mistake a roadside inn for your true destination.
The Imperial Palace: Pure Land is originally attained through loyalty and filial piety; the Golden Terrace’s superior grade is the result of fundamental merit (Confucianism).
In the Daoist practice of *banyun* (internal alchemy), effort is excessive while accomplishment is meager. One must understand that immortals are not truly immortal (*Lengyan Jing* states:

"Furthermore, there are those who do not rely on correct enlightenment but cultivate *samādhi* by separately practicing deluded thoughts, maintaining mental images to solidify the physical form, and roaming in mountain forests where humans cannot reach; these are the ten kinds of immortals, whose lifespan lasts a thousand [years]").

"Ten thousand years! This too is saṃsāra; it is the wandering of deluded thoughts. When the retribution is exhausted, one returns once more to enter the various realms of existence. One must know that only in the Pure Land is there eternal life.

(The Dharma Master Tanluan of the Later Wei dynasty initially received ten fascicles of the *Cinnabar Scripture* from the Immortal Tao Hongjing and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of alchemy. Later, he encountered Bodhiruci, who asked him, "Does the Buddha-way contain the art of long life? Bodhiruci replied, "Long life and immortality—this is my Buddha-way.

He then gave him the *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations*, saying, "If you study this, you shall no longer be born within the Three Realms nor go forth among the Six Paths. Your lifespan will be inexhaustible. Thereupon, Tanluan burned the immortal scriptures and devoted himself exclusively to the cultivation of the *Contemplation Sutra*. [Holding gold to] make...

A gold bracelet never changes; playing with bubbles to make beads yields only a name. (Someone asked: "I study the arts of the immortals and thus attain longevity in this very life. You recite the Buddha's name, yet you die in this very body. Where, then, is your longevity? He replied:

"You cling to this illusory body as if it were solid, like playing with bubbles to make beads—there is a name, but no reality. I know that the nature of the mind is truly eternal, like holding gold to make a bracelet—it never undergoes change.

Furthermore, the lifespan of an immortal lasts a thousand years and is easily exhausted, like playing with bubbles to make beads. In the Western Land, a lifespan measured by kalpas is difficult to fathom, like holding gold to make a bracelet. He sent word: "Those who study the arts of the immortals should instead practice mindfulness of the Buddha.")
The Lotus Pond is truly superior to Mount Penglai (Daoism).
Seeking office, one often laments that one’s rank is low. As rank grows higher, the situation becomes increasingly precarious. The uncut jade is ashamed before the beautiful gem;
The mud-dragging tail envies the auspicious tortoise. Knowing that official service is empty and tasteless, Try reciting the name of Amitābha.
Who is this? Though you may be busy with official documents, set them aside for a moment. It is not fitting to neglect the "Ten Recitations" every morning. (As for the Ten Recitations:

every day at dawn, stand facing west upright, join your palms, and chant the name of Amitābha Buddha with a continuous voice. One full breath constitutes one recitation; ten such breaths are called the Ten Recitations. For as long as this life lasts, they must not be abandoned for even a single day.
If you can do so, rebirth [in the Pure Land] is certain. △ (Official).
The retired scholar flees fame far from the bustling markets; this body dwells in pure seclusion amidst the emerald peaks. Half a moon is shared across the ridges;
a whole mountain rests against the pillow at the head of the bed. To dwell in a thatched cottage in poverty is but a temporary plan;
who knows if one will return upon the path of the setting sun? Deep within the Lotus Buddha-land, the fragrant traces of world-transcendence are beyond reach. (Yin)
Artisans succeed easily when they dwell in their workshops; each craft has its own specialty and is distinct from others.

To turn the divine artistry within one’s hands, and to reclaim the Creator within one’s breast—this destiny has never been fashioned by another; there is only the mind that can be mastered by oneself.
Content with whatever lot one’s wife and children bring, may we all gather in harmony to recite the Buddha’s name together. (Work)
Merchants travel the roads for years on end; their boats and carriages speed along, always pressing for time. Deeply moved by profit, they fail to perceive the dangers of wind and waves;

burdened by heavy goods, they treat their own lives as light. They harbor long-standing regrets that their goods are too many to fetch a high price, yet they do not realize that once the body dies, it cannot be reborn.
I urge you to recite the Buddha’s name and return to the West; compared to the pleasures of this Sahā world, that merit will be ten thousand times greater. (Shāng)
The livelihood of the fisherman rests upon his small boat; south, north, east, and west, he goes as he pleases.
He cleaves the moonlight as he lowers his oars to the depths, and brings the mountain scenery up onto the bow of his vessel. He constantly bids his wife and children spread out nets;

who recognizes that this old man is casting down his fishing hook? The ocean of suffering is boundless—do not sink into its depths! Rely early upon the power of the Buddha to repent for your deep transgressions. (Yu)
The woodcutter’s home lies at the edge of the azure mountains; amidst the sound of his axe, he fells tangled firewood. He hews through the roots of clouds and pierces the veins of the earth;
he cleaves the jagged teeth of rock to reveal the lips of the peaks. Behold the old tombs where withered bones lie buried;
see not the new graves where the dead rise again. Turn back early to seek the path of escape; it is well to hide one's body within the womb of the lotus. (Woodcutter)
The farmer chants the Buddha’s name with earnest devotion; Turning about, he plants fresh seedlings with his own hands.
A single straw hat parts the willow rain; One plow furrows through the apricot-blossom clouds. With arms bent, he eats his fill, rejoicing in the ripening autumn;
Turning his head, he longs for home, gazing at the evening glow. A single expanse of lapis lazuli fields is beautiful; Naturally so, requiring no further tilling.
All the myriad affairs of the world are but floating dust; only poetry and the classics can truly satisfy the human spirit. A thousand scrolls by the western window under the waning moon;
several volumes by the eastern pavilion amidst the wild mountains of spring. The sound of chanting is not as fine as the sound of the Buddha;
the flavor of the books is no match for the true flavor of the Way. Once you have realized the pure land of your own mind, the dregs of literary composition are not worth setting forth.
The first class of worldly people cultivate meritorious deeds, hoping to become high officials in future lives.

Even if one’s rank were as exalted as the Five Marquises, how could it compare to being born into a lowly station? Giving water merely nourishes the seeds of greed (giving alms out of a desire for wealth and honor);

yet the sprouts of goodness instead grow into the roots and stems of karma (attracting wealth and honor through giving, creating further karma through that wealth and honor, and falling once more into the three miserable realms). I pray that you may turn away from existence.

Outflows become non-outflows. (By dedicating these meritorious deeds toward the Western [Pure Land], they immediately become non-outflows. One’s name shall early be inscribed as the foremost among the blossoms.

(In this land, through the practice of *nien-fo*, one shall immediately produce a single lotus flower within the Seven-Jeweled Pond of the West; one’s name shall be inscribed upon it, and after death, one shall be reborn therein. △ (Cultivating Merit).

When the single mind goes astray, one encounters a fork in the road; one composes scriptures and establishes a fundamental school of one's own (referring to the present-day five sections and six volumes, all of which are plagiarized from Buddhist sutras and mixed with vulgar language to form their own canons).
At the side of two doors, secret formulas are transmitted; in a village of three households, a crowd of the ignorant gathers.

The path to the Land of Bliss is originally level and straight; the Buddha-dharma is impartial and fundamentally most just. I earnestly exhort you to turn back your heads and return to the orthodox teaching.
Amida Buddha: In every thought-moment, perceive the true void (the outsider’s path).
Nishi: Recite the Buddha’s name well, following conditions as they arise. Do not wander through every corner of the deep inner chambers. Maintain pure poverty for yourself as your medicine.

Cease striving for deluded blessings, lest you incur further transgression. (An ancient said: "The merit of conditioned effort abounds with faults; before heaven is attained, hell is already formed. The Root of Sentiment.

Severing [defilements] like withered silk from a lotus root, the essence of her precepts is as fragrant as a lotus emerging from the water. In days to come, when her spirit dwells in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, she shall pay homage to the Golden Immortal (the Buddha) upon the ponds of the seven treasures. (For the Bhikṣuṇī).
O poor man, do not hesitate to recite the Buddha’s name. The cravings within the belly of cold and hunger are easy to remove.

At the hearth, the sun slants while smoke has not yet risen; at the roof’s edge, dew falls as the bedding remains empty. Deeply knowing this realm to be a prison-bar, one utterly loathes this carcass as a festering abscess.
With infinite celestial robes and various transformed foods, you shall dwell at ease in the Land of Ultimate Bliss in years to come. (Poor)
In the ways of the household, there is no need for boastful rivalry with rival states; from the beginning, virtue has been honored and gold and bronze held in contempt.

Among those of peerless wealth, none surpassed Yuan Xian; as for the foremost among the poor, it was none other than Shi Chong. Though he possessed thousands of chests left to his descendants, he could not bring even a single thing before King Yan.
How much better it is to recite the Buddha’s name and be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*); the wealth of one's own nature is fundamentally inexhaustible.
Though a nobleman be honored, it is not yet cause for joy; after death, he returns to but a single grave. In the gardens and pavilions of the Three Xies, the swallows are gone;
at the gates of the Five Marquises, there is only cold cloud. Only when one ascends to the superior grade is one truly noble; only when the mind awakens to True Suchness does one establish merit.
Returning to the Lotus Pond, look back once more: the worldly ants are all in a frantic swarm. (Noble)
Past karma has now summoned this lowly body; from time immemorial, my brows and eyes have never been raised. For many years I have labored in hardship, always following my master;

throughout my life I have worked diligently, never daring to resent others. It is best to apply oneself to the diligent recitation of the Buddha’s name; it is most fitting for the spirit to dwell alone in the Pure Land.
When the time comes, one shall join the assembly at the Lotus Pond, attaining sainthood and transcending the mundane, a nobility beyond compare.
The karmic consciousness of the wise person constantly curves and turns; they should strive to erase all former thoughts. Within these six characters there is no calculation;

beyond the single sound of "Buddha," all mechanisms cease. When the nature of things is seen through, who would fear death? Though one may be capable in many worldly affairs, one simply lacks leisure.
Ultimately, rebirth in the Pure Land is the superior strategy; seek the path home early, for you shall know how to return. (Zhi)
For those of literary talent whose wisdom is their vocation, the Way is easily accomplished. Cease boasting of your ingenuity and pride yourself on your cleverness;

a few verses are not enough to satisfy hunger, and half a word has never been able to oppose birth and death. Let flowery speech be transformed into words of truth, and let the sound of chanting be turned into the resonance of suffering and emptiness.
In the Land of Bliss there are many excellent compositions; even the waterbirds and the wind-swayed branches can all join in the chorus. (Hui)
Fools commit transgressions, indulging freely in greed and anger; they refuse to believe in the relationship between cause and effect from the outset.

They claim there is no future life beyond this present existence, yet they know that today will be followed by tomorrow. (Someone asked: "Tomorrow can be seen, but who can see the future life? He replied: "The divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) can see it. Since you lack the divine eye, [you cannot see it]. )

Furthermore, because they do not believe the Buddha’s words, they do not see the next world. Again he asked: "What are the characteristics that the divine eye can perceive? He replied: "It is like seeing a person emerge from one room and enter another; dying here and being born there is exactly the same. One has just moved house yet still speaks of the former one;
one has barely changed clothes yet does not recognize the person. The gateway of birth and death is truly painful and urgent.
I urge you to practice the mindfulness of the Buddha without wearying of its frequency. (Foolish!)
The deluded person, nearing old age, knows not to cease; calling out in a daze, they do not turn their head. A virulent illness treats the physician with malice;
a chronic ailment turns its back on the medicine as an enemy. The rope of craving easily binds like a bird cast into a cage;
the bait of desire can pull a fish onto the hook. I urge you: awaken early to the conditions of this world; even now, you may still cast yourself as a seed into the lotus pond. (Chí)
In this world there are but many who suffer; having created new calamities for themselves, what can be done? Wild weeds cover the ground where spring never reaches;
with a body bound in shackles, the night is hard to pass. To cry out in grievance, do not call upon Heaven or Earth;
when calling for relief from pain, you ought to mind the Buddha. The three realms have always been a prison; I urge you to leave *Sahā* (the world of suffering) as soon as possible.
Do not say that the pleasures of the human world are abundant; from the beginning, when joy reaches its peak, sorrow arises. With willows and flowers filling the city, one brings fine guests along;
throughout the night, pipes and songs resound as one carouses in the painted towers. One only perceives the wine upon one’s face, yet who knows that death lies at one's very heels?
The Western Pure Land is truly a place of bliss; simply recite the name of Amitābha, and you shall go there to roam.
The leisurely person reciting the Buddha’s name dwells in ease; Do not cast your precious time into the void. In old age, letters arrive and the hair grows white;
When death comes, there is no official decree, and life cannot be retained. Prepare your provisions in advance while you still have the body;

Cease worrying for children and grandchildren with eyes that see them. Your home is in the Land of Bliss—return there is best; There, clothing and food are provided naturally, requiring no seeking. (Leisure)
I urge you to practice mindfulness of the Buddha; there is no time for idleness. By the time you achieve leisure, illness will have already appeared before you.

When the mind falls into confusion, you must keep your eyes open; when thoughts arise amidst busyness, you must apply the whip. To enter a thousand-fold army with a single blade, or to pass a ladle of water into a hundred-boiling cauldron—this is what it takes.
The Buddha does not obstruct your busyness; rather, it is your own busyness that obstructs you. Therefore, from this very day, serve the Golden Immortal. (Busyness)
In youth, practice the nembutsu with true spirit; do not wait until old age and decline to seek the ford. Green grass half-buries the bones of those once fair of countenance;
in the Yellow Springs, many are seen who were once black-haired youths. The Dragon Maiden who offered the pearl quickly attained Buddhahood;
Sudhana who sought the Way returned to realize the Truth. Once the news of impermanence arrives, what cause will there be for regret? (Shao)
The light of years in one’s final stage is piteously short; like a flash of lightning or a bubble on water, it lasts but a moment.

As yellow leaves gradually wither, one is truly old; the autumn wind is about to arrive—how can one endure such sorrow? Without artifice, do not crave this floating world; though you have a mouth, you should only contemplate the Buddha.
Cherish yourself as you approach your departure and must exert effort; do not allow yourself to waste away through negligence for ten thousand kalpas.

The origin of illness is itself the remedy; one deeply understands that birth and death are impermanent. Having endured severe punishments in the sorrowful prisons, and having tasted intense suffering, one grows weary of this skin-sack.
Moment by moment, contemplate Amitābha and do not turn your back on awakening; thought after thought, aspire for Sukhāvatī and wish to return home.
When shall I attain a body of pure emptiness, with a lifespan as immeasurable as the sands of the Ganges? (Illness)

At the time of death, do not allow yourself to be needlessly terrified. (For those who recite the Buddha’s name, the foremost thing to avoid is the fear of death. If one fears death, one will not attain rebirth in the Pure Land.

There are many who spend their entire lives reciting the Buddha’s name, yet at the end of life they focus solely on taking medicine and seeking physicians, never mentioning the matter of rebirth. This is the fault of fearing death. With diligent mindfulness directed toward that direction, the pus and blood are gradually cast off from the skin-sack;
the foul-smelling, tattered garments are about to be shed. The afflictions of many lifetimes are truly like a chronic malady; with a single phrase of Maitreya...
Ta is the Medicine King. The ocean of suffering is deep and vast; seek only to escape it. Do not worry that the Buddha will not launch the compassionate vessel (to ferry you across).
At dawn, during the hour of the Tiger (3–5 a.m.), when the weather is clear, the light of the eastern sky has just begun to arise. The Dharma-body was previously unmanifest and remained in darkness;
now that the eye of wisdom has just opened, one begins to see the light. How can one fail to depart for the Land of Bliss this very day? Take all deluded habits and—
In times of peace, I think afar of the assembly of sages who made offerings to the Buddha; they held flowers in their hands, contained within their robes (at the hour of the Tiger).
At the hour of the Rabbit, the sun rises and the air is vast and azure; the myriad phenomena are clearly manifest, nothing hidden. Amidst the thick mists, the reflections of flowers are disordered;
within the ranks of red dust, horse hooves are in haste. I imagine that everywhere there are blossoms of blue lotuses; as my mindfulness matures, at every moment there is the Great [Awakening].
O King of Awakening, wait until the birthless gives rise to the pure land; let the light of a single hair-pore pervade the entire realm of sands (the hour of the Rabbit).
At mealtime, smoke rises from ten thousand households; from of old, the gap between the poor and the wealthy has been too vast. In thatched huts, even coarse grain and husks are not sustained;

yet in noble mansions, even wine and meat are met with loathing. Suffering and joy in dreams are originally without reality; it is only after awakening that the body and mind truly begin [to perceive].

It does not shift. At this time, one should sit and eat in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*). From afar, one knows that the hundred flavors appear before one (at the hour of *śi*, the morning watch).
At the hour of *si* (the mid-morning watch), the shadow of the sun falls upon the *yu-zhong* position; it is precisely so, yet there remains a slight discrepancy of a fraction of an inch.

When right mindfulness awakens, there is still the trace of awakening; where the deluded mind is empty, emptiness itself has not yet been forgotten. Among the heterodox and the biased, which is not the central truth? Who among people is not partial and crooked?
Supreme Impartiality. Gathering those of the three faculties to return to the Pure Land, he directly causes the myriad streams to all flow toward the source (the hour of the Snake).
When the sun’s orb is at its zenith in the middle of the sky, all things high and low are seen in their entirety.

Within the Avīci Hell is the true Pure Land; inside the body of a dung beetle is the Golden Immortal. How truly pitiable is the wayward son who has lost his home; how deluded is the child who has turned his back on his father. Faith...
How pitiable! Only today do I know how to return to my native village. At the hour of noon (wu), the fields from the beginning of the kalpa remain as they were.
At the hour of un (wei), the sun first slants outside the window; the shadows of flowers in disarray fall upon the green gauze.
Two-thirds of the passage of time has already passed; how can the span of a hundred-year life have no end? Dwelling here for a while is not my true land; I look far back toward the West.
My home is the Land of Ultimate Bliss, where the people are of Immeasurable Life. There, one does not calculate the passage of years by the sun and moon (the hour of *wei*).
At the hour of *pu*, when evening falls and it is precisely the hour of *shen*, the consciousness of karma becomes vast and empty, losing its original truth.

Within Jambudvīpa there are many matters of suffering; within the Sahā world there are few people at leisure. When poison is placed within one's food, how can one know to avoid it? After the itch arises, one scratches the sore—how could this possibly...?
Wearied by frequency, as the day fades, I drift alone and do not return; in vain do I weary my kin who lean upon their gates, their hopes severed (the hour of Shen).
At the hour of You, I remember the Buddha with deep longing; leaning solitary upon the tower, my two shoulders hunched high. My eyes follow the floating clouds into the azure void;
my mind accompanies the white sun as it descends into the blue heavens. Beyond the world of heaven and earth, there is no one else to go; how could there be a letter arriving from a wild goose?
Beside the wild geese, sitting long, one does not realize that day has already set. One suspects instead that the body is within a lotus of the Jade Pond (the hour of You).

At the hour of Xu, let all affairs be left unspoken; one must maintain the mindfulness of impermanence at every thought. When the great limit suddenly arrives, it is truly a pitch-black night; the dark barrier knows nothing of the setting of the sun.
To hold a prayer bead and easily recite the Buddha’s name while alive is easy; but to cut paper and attempt to summon the dead is difficult.
The soul departs later; prepare your provisions in advance so you may return early. Do not let yourself face regret on the path ahead with no way out (the hour of Xu).
At the hour of Hai, when people settle for the night and clamor ceases, sternly discipline body and mind; do not be arrogant. Cut off the deluded mind as if mowing down green grass;
push aside the darkness of ignorance as if climbing a high mountain. Tears flow because of recollecting the Buddha, utterly beyond restraint; sorrow arises from thinking of home.
Easily dissolved. Gazing afar at the calyx of the white lotus flower, one surely knows that its name has already been inscribed (at the hour of Hai).
At midnight, the hour of Zi, all movement ceases; yin and yang alternate and revolve in mutual circulation.

A single solitary moon amidst the dreams of a thousand households; a few lingering stars across ten thousand miles of heaven. Earth naturally manifests itself as form—how could there be anything external? The Buddha appears from the mind; he is fundamentally...

Boundless. When will the suffering of perpetual flux be forever extinguished? At the hour of the Ox (1–3 a.m.), when emerging from the sheath of the body within the flower, one rises from sleep at the crowing of the cock at dawn during the final watch of the night and puts on one's robes; thus recollecting with clarity, before a single thought arises, the True Buddha appears.
As soon as the myriad conditions stir, they become mere provisional names. Knowing that conditions are not real, what obstacle can there be? Realizing that delusion has no basis, thoughts [subside].
Spontaneously peaceful, how could body and mind not return to the Ultimate Bliss? In true emptiness and illusory existence, all is unborn (the hour of the Ox).
The first month of the spring king is the New Year; every household sets out wine and feasts to celebrate. Ten thousand households sing and play the flute in places of pleasure;
The streets are filled with blossoming flowers and a sky lit by rising lanterns. The scenery before one’s eyes cannot remain beautiful forever; Yet the splendor beyond the kalpas is naturally so.
It does not shift; in the peaceful land of the ancestral home, there are no wax candles. Branch upon branch they illuminate one another—the lotus blossoms of the Jade Pond (the first month).
Now that it is the second month, the scenery is worthy of praise. One should mindfully recite the name of Amitābha while enjoying the splendor of the flowers:

the pale white pear blossoms have just begun to open their buds; the light yellow willow catkins have newly sprouted their shoots. In the shop of the oriole, light smoke and thin mist linger; amidst the fine rain and gentle breeze, the swallows appear.
My son, how can this compare to the beautiful lands of one’s native home? In rows of seven, the *piṅgala* birds call out (February). The clear spring of the third month passes in a fleeting glance.
What is there not to cause heartache? What is it but sorrow? With wind and rain filling the city, songs are few;
For ten li of mountain tombs, the sounds of wailing are many. Seize the opportunity while still alive to cultivate pure karma; Do not let yourself harbor resentment at the moment of death.
Yama. The spring colors of one’s hometown remain ever-present; one can imagine lotus flowers emerging from the ripples (the third month).

In the mountains and forests of the fourth month, there is little dust; reflecting upon Amitābha, there is no need for companions. Having newly shed their plain robes, they cast off their silken sheaths;
scattering golden pellets, they cause the yellow plum blossoms to fall. To be a traveler at the end of one's journey is truly bitter; for the profligate who longs for home, it is most [painful].
How pitiable! I reckon the Compassionate Honored One must be mindful of me, stretching out his hand every morning as I await my return (in the fourth month).

In the fifth month, the scene of the Dragon Boat Festival is particularly striking; the racing of dragon boats has been handed down through all ages. A few stalks of *phrag* leaves are whetted like swords;
