a single tree of *dāruharidrā* flowers is as if about to burst into flame. When will there be a day of escape from the boundless sea of suffering? How many paths lead to the Land of Bliss?
Returning at that time to the place where the waters of the Jade Pond swirl in eddies, fragrant breezes blow in successive waves over white lotuses (the fifth month).
In the sixth month, the seasonal air of the human world is high; the blazing house of fire is consumed by flames. Shadows from a grove of trees conceal a lofty pavilion;

lotus blossoms for ten *li* reflect upon a painted bridge. The sound of chanting the Buddha’s name is mournful and frequently brings tears; the longing for one's homeland is so intense it increases further.
How weary! When shall I return to the Clear Cool Pool? The waters abound, washing away the weariness of my breast (June).
In the new autumn of the seventh month, the air first grows cool; the sticky heat is about to end, and the nights grow longer. On all four walls, the dark wind whistles as crickets chirp;

across the single pool of withered grass, the *hanjiang* insects cry out. At the deep of night, leaning against the railing, I gaze at the waning moon; at the thin twilight, I push open the window and look out.
Twilight. Long have I wandered the traveler’s road, drifting far and wide. I pray with earnest devotion for the Buddha’s power to return home soon (in the seventh month).
Mid-autumn in the eighth month brings a slight chill; dew falls thick and fast upon the weeds. From a single tree, the fragrance of osmanthus leaks forth;
across ten thousand homes, the shadows of the bright moon form a perfect circle. I long for my native land, yet no news arrives; several times I have wished to soar aloft, but lack the strength.
Wings and feathers; the rows upon rows of trees embrace the Buddha-lands. When shall we personally lean against the jade balustrades to gaze?
(August) The scenery on the Double Ninth is particularly expansive. I gather *zhuyu* myself and brew tea. Red brocade adorns a thousand trees of leaves;
yellow gold opens fully across one hedge of flowers. Whenever I ascend the mountain peak to look toward my homeland, I then climb to the top of the tower to gaze afar.
Thus, the old family home. One imagines seeing within the ponds of the seven treasures, branch after branch of lotuses as large as chariots (in the ninth month).
The tenth month has always been known as "Little Spring. Peach blossoms, red, have just burst open on a new branch. I gaze long upon old tombs as they take on new forms;
whenever I see a new person escorting an old one away, for ten thousand kalpas of birth and death, who would stir their thoughts? In this life of a hundred years, I am alone.

It wounds the spirit. Turn your head, and it is the path to the Western Land. It only requires that one’s vow-power be sincere (the tenth month). At the ends of the earth, once more the Yang is seen to arise.

As the six tubes send forth the drifting ash, the seasonal breath shifts; grain by grain the cold pepper and plum begin to break open, and point by point the tender jade-like willow is about to sprout.
The nights are long and dreams of returning home are easily found; yet at the end of the year, it is difficult to compose [this poem].

The Sentiments of a Traveler A journey of over a hundred thousand leagues to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang), My heart, bright and persistent, hangs upon the long star (Venus) [in the eleventh month].
The year ends and time reaches its limit—this is most grievous. Gloomy clouds darken the sky as the days stretch on in vain. The wind strips the myriad trees bare like bleached bones;
Snow covers the ten thousand mountains, turning them all white-headed. I see only that the rush to pass the New Year is like a speeding arrow; Who among us is in such haste to leave suffering behind?
Like an enemy, how can one bear to remain lingering in this Sahā world? Another year (twelve months) has passed within the time of a dream.
Ever since being bound by the causes of karma in the Sahā world, many lifetimes of wandering have been truly bitter and painful. In an instant one leaves a house only to enter another;
with such rapidity one discards a body only to receive another again. One has once been a king or nobleman contending for kingdoms and cities, and several times has perished for the sake of ants.
Dust and grime! If you do not contemplate returning this time, you will continue as before to suffer within the wheel of rebirth.
The gate of vows of Amitābha, our compassionate father, stands open; he gathers in all living beings as if they were one child.

Departing from the stench and filth within the mass of pus and blood, you shall receive a womb amidst the fragrance of lotus flowers. Rely solely upon pure vows as your excellent guide; let only doubt be the obstacle.
Discarded Materiality. This turbid and evil Sahā world is difficult to dwell in for long; let us quickly join our virtuous friends in chanting the "Return" (Gui Lai).
A Poem on the Eight Sufferings.
The winds of karma blow consciousness into the womb; hidden deep within the prison gates, it is truly pitiable. Whenever hunger strikes, one is hung upside down;
repeatedly startled by coarse food pressing down like a mountain. Even Śrāvakas reach this state with their minds still obscured; Bodhisattvas therein have not yet opened their wisdom.
Vowing to sever the ties of affection, they are born in Sukhāvatī; from amidst the lotuses, they emerge as jade infants.

In old age, I am surpassed in all matters by others and have withdrawn from the world; my physical form brings me shame, lacking the vigor of youth. Once the rosy complexion has vanished, it leaves no trace;
new white hairs gradually appear like frost. Shedding tears, I secretly recall the joys of childhood; seeing others, I can only speak of my own prime in vain.
My years are advanced. Who would have known that the spring of the Pure Land remains forever, never allowing body and mind to be busily occupied day or night?

When the four great elements of this body happen for a moment to fall into disorder, there is no plan by which this frame can be restored. Like a fading lamp leaving but a shadow behind, it cannot be preserved.
A Dream: Night raindrops fall with melancholy as the void fills the streets. Where have all past joys and pleasures gone? In this present moment of bitter pain, who can truly comprehend it?
Who would have known that the essence of ultimate bliss is pure and empty, Wandering freely upon the white jade steps?
The consciousness of one about to die is suddenly extinguished by impermanence; the four elements separate, difficult to control. Like a tortoise shedding its shell, the pain is utterly absolute;
like a crab falling into boiling water, one is filled with frantic terror. Willingly accepting the prison gates as companions, one stands with hands bound at the dark barrier.
The King of Ghosts: How is it that the flowers bloom and one personally beholds the Buddha? Without birth or extinction, his lifespan is difficult to measure.

The pain born of separation from those we love and the parting from death is most grievous; every word spoken makes one’s heart ache as if to break. [This concludes] the parting words of Lady Yu within her curtained chamber to Xiang Yu.

Feathers flutter as the Princess of Bing bows her thanks to the Sovereign from atop her horse. Her tears are deeper than rivers and seas, yet she still deems them shallow; her resentment reaches further than heaven and earth, yet she finds it not long enough.
May we all gather at the place where those of supreme goodness meet, and pray that through vast kalpas we shall never be parted.

The suffering of encountering those one hates is something all people desire to avoid; who would have known that past karma would summon them together? With wealth, it is hard to buy the pardon of the Lord of Yama;
with no stratagem, one cannot seek leniency from the wardens of hell. When his army was defeated, Zhang Xun thought of becoming a ghost; when his life ended, Lady Xiao vowed—
I have become a cat; when shall I be permitted to join the assembly at the Lotus Pond? Let the enmities of accumulated kalpas be extinguished together.

In seeking what one cannot obtain, whether in poverty or success, there is always a karmic cause from former lives. The more one harbors hope, the more one becomes negligent; though I raise my sails, I repeatedly see my boat sink.

Guest: Hanging up the placard especially hurts those who fail the examination; though they till the soil all their lives, it is hard to fill their bellies. Though they spin and weave for many years, they still wear robes of rags.
In the Land of Bliss, clothing and food are naturally excellent; there is no need for such petty toil and suffering.
The five aggregates (skandhas)—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are ablaze. Form is the body; the other four are the mind. "Ablaze" means burning and intensifying.
Oppressive to both body and mind, the miseries are many. There is no place for the sound of lamentation to cry out. Where the liver and intestines are severed, the feelings are hard to sever;
when blood and tears have dried, the resentment has not yet dried. Having served as an envoy at the sea for twenty years, a single night crossing the pass turned my hair white.
O Head, when shall I practice meditative contemplation in the Pure Land? May stillness and illumination arise simultaneously, transcending both existence and non-existence.
In this verse of aspiration, I prostrate to Śākyamuni, the Lord who teaches the Dharma in this Sahā world; I take refuge in Amitāyus, the Guide of the Pure Land.
Now, relying upon the power of the Buddha, I shall propagate the teachings of the Pure Land. I have composed one hundred and eight verses, each consisting of eight lines.
To accord with the capacities of those in this region, I have expounded them in verse. Should the words I have spoken contradict the Buddhas, [may I be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss].
Those who deceive and mislead the world shall undergo the sufferings of hell for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of kalpas, yet even then they will not reach their end.
If this were not so, may you each fortunately give rise to true faith; be careful not to harbor doubt or suspicion, nor to develop overweening pride.
And by means of the pride of inferiority—through these two types of mind, one brings about the loss of one's own wholesome benefits.
I pray that all who see or hear this will exhort one another in turn; if one exhorts even a single person, or even many people, the merit thereof is inconceivable.
Metaphors cannot fully describe it. By this merit, may it reach all beings; may we and all sentient beings be reborn together in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.

Verses on the Contemplation of Impurity (with Preface) The Buddha taught the contemplation of impurity for the sake of sentient beings who are overcome by desire. By contemplating it for a long time, desire is eliminated;

thus one may cross the river of craving and transcend the ocean of suffering. While dwelling in leisure, I read the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* and, taking its essential meaning, [composed these verses].
I have composed this verse for myself as a reminder, and to likewise warn the world:
The thought of death (one should first practice this visualization as the foundation for the nine subsequent contemplations):
All that is cherished comes to an end; how can this body endure forever? To shed tears on behalf of another in vain—who understands the need for such reflection?

The visualization of bloating: One recalls the lush beauty of youth, which has suddenly become a bloated corpse. As for those who were once young before one’s eyes—what has become of their appearance now? The visualization of livid discoloration:
The features of red and white are clearly distinct; the body is mottled blue and yellow, putrid and decayed. I beg you to open your eyes and look: these are not two different kinds of people.

Once the skin and flesh have fallen away through the perception of decay, the five viscera are revealed within. Relying on you to look thoroughly to the bottom, where is there anything worth lingering over?

In the visualization of the bloody path, one perceives that the rosy complexion no longer remains; there is only the residue of dark red blood smeared upon it. When one seeks to discern the features of beauty or ugliness, the physical form gradually becomes blurred. This is the visualization of the festering pus.
This putrid mass would be difficult to behold; its stench and filth would be unbearable to smell. Who could have known that where pus now festers was once perfumed with orchids and musk?

One who contemplates eating thinks of sheep and dogs devouring human flesh, yet humans have likewise eaten dogs and sheep. Not knowing the distinction between human and beast, who is foul and who is fragrant?

The visualization of the dismembered body: once the limbs are scattered, the hands and feet are gradually moved apart. Contemplate their lovely form intently; where, in the end, does it return? This is the visualization of the bones (*asthi-saṃjñā*).
This was originally but a skeleton, which once deceived and deluded people. In the past it appeared to be real; today, upon seeing it, it is revealed as truly so.
As the power of the imagined fire blazes fiercely, the remaining remains suddenly vanish. Observe within the smoke and flames: can greed ever find a place to abide?
The previous poem merely indicated the general outline; as it has not yet been thoroughly examined and contemplated, I have composed another five-character regulated verse to expand upon it.
Contemplation on Death (Maraṇasaṃjñā)
That which was loved has been parted from forever; its desolation is unbearable to behold. Consciousness has just left the old body; the corpse has already descended into the empty coffin.
The night fire leaves the hall cold and empty; the autumn wind makes the white curtains chill. I urge you, while you still possess this life, to first contemplate the moment of death.
The wind element swells within, causing it to distend in an instant; the body becomes like a bag filled with water, and the belly resembles a gourd severed from its vine.

Deeply smeared with filth and grease, it is like charcoal in the dark, while flies and maggots swarm over it like sand. Having been deceived by this thin skin, one now regrets the errors of former years.

The wind of the perception of bluish discoloration has blown upon and scorched them for many days; their greenish-yellow hues are truly pitiable. Their skin is parched like a rotting tangerine; their bones are decayed, half as withered as old rafters.

Though ears and noses are missing, they remain in place; though tendons and limbs are severed, they are joined again. Though a stone statue does not speak, it too sheds tears when confronted with this.

When the skin is destroyed and just begins to fall away, the physical form is already beset by injury. The flesh splits open like a half-ripened melon; snakes bore through as if to emerge from the entrails.
Withered vines entwine the disheveled hair; moss and lichen rot the garments. I send word to you, O beautiful lady: do not carry this sack of excrement painted with art.

A vision of blood-stained, heartless slabs—throughout a thousand autumns, no person shall rise from them. Dripping and soaking, they smear the withered grass; in disarray, they defile the dust and soil.
One cannot distinguish between beauty and ugliness; how could one know a male or female body? Alas for these deluded physical eyes, which mistake the false for the true!

The visualization of festering pus is like thin skin soaked through by broken paper; it is like rotting flesh discarded in stale soup. Pus and blood erupt from within, while flies and maggots swarm from without.

It is as easy to vomit at the sight of pig intestines as it is difficult to clear the water used to wash a dog. Were it not for this profound sense of revulsion, how could one sever deluded attachments?
Devouring the thought of a corpse, one encounters being devoured; not even a fraction of one's heart remains whole. It cannot satisfy the hunger of crows, nor dry the drool of greedy dogs.
In former years you cherished it in vain; on this day, who will pity you? It is not worth even the price of pork or mutton.
When one disperses their thoughts, the four limbs suddenly fall apart; from where does this single body come? It is not only that one’s physical form is lost, but even one’s name becomes empty.
One observes the tall and short as autumn grasses; one asks the late wind about the thick and slender. I ask you to cast your eyes upward and examine this matter with meticulous scrutiny.
The skin and flesh have already crumbled away; only the bones remain. Rain adds to the hue of the moss and lichens; water drenches the traces of the sand above.
Many insects and ants pull and drag at them; few descendants remain to preserve them. Where has their elegance gone? It grieves the souls that have not yet returned home.
Visualize the blazing flames of incineration resting upon withered bones; in an instant they burn fiercely. Red sparks fly toward the horizon, and black smoke penetrates the treetops.
Forgetfulness is reduced to ash, while the true mind hangs like the sun. To transcend the path of birth and death, this contemplation must be studied with diligence.
Verses on the Four Foundations of Mindfulness (with Preface):
When the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa, he entrusted all bhikṣus to abide by the four foundations of mindfulness, saying they should be no different from the Buddha himself.

Now, as we dwell in the age of the Dharma’s decay, those with right mindfulness are few. Looking upon this dharma-gate, who is there to practice and study it? Is it not merely that people fail to contemplate it?

As for its meaning, I have yet to fully comprehend its name; how can one help but sigh in admiration? While dwelling in the mountains with nothing to do, I read the "Chapter on the Bequeathed Teaching" from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Thereupon, I have taken its essence and set it to musical meter, so that those who chant it may increase their right mindfulness and extinguish deluded thoughts.
I have placed this by my seat to admonish myself daily, and I shall not forget these bequeathed instructions.

Contemplating the impurity of the body, one gives rise to a single inverted perception; thus there arises this illusory causal body. Pus and blood constantly mingle and flow together; its stench and filth are ever laid bare:

paper-like membranes adhere to the skin that wraps the flesh, while vines bind the bones and sinews. Hairs cover it in dense clusters like weeds, and insects dwell in every nook and cranny as neighbors.
Within, there is nothing but stench and filth; without, there is merely clothing and headwear. The four elements are fundamentally without reality; how could the sense organs possess any truth?
Speech is but the resonance of wind; movement is the circulation of breath. We forcibly designate them as "man" or "woman," establishing "host" and "guest" through empty names.
A hundred years, three feet of earth; ten thousand ages, a single mound of dust. Noble and base alike turn their heads in vain; the wise and the foolish both grieve their spirits.
Born in vain and dying in vain—who can recognize the person of original nature?

Contemplating that sensation is suffering, from where do all sufferings arise? One deeply understands that attachment to sensation is the root: as soon as one experiences what is favorable or unfavorable, grasping and rejecting follow in every direction.
Where there is abundance, decline inevitably follows; where there is no glory or disgrace, nothing is achieved. Enmity emerges from within those closest; sorrow is born from the midst of joy.
The Wangs have departed; where is their home? The houses of Cao and Liu have already collapsed. How many cycles of joy and sorrow are but dreams? Victory and defeat are but a single chessboard.
Affairs run contrary to the heart; poverty and illness merge together. The "God of Wealth" cannot be summoned; the "Ghost of Poverty" departs with difficulty.
What benefit is there in constant anxiety? What use is restless discontent? Without seeking, one is humble yet noble; by knowing contentment, what is lacking is made full.
If one awakens to the principle of true emptiness, where can sorrow or joy sprout?

Contemplating the mind as impermanent, one sees that the deluded mind has no place of abiding. As for its essence and characteristics, how are they? It is like a flickering candle in the wind, or a trembling wave upon the water.

Each family’s gate is distinct (the six sense organs), yet the six brothers are many (the six consciousnesses). They are restless, each racing and contending—just as the eye pursues forms and the ear pursues sounds.

Sounds and the like are all in disarray and never harmonize; (just as the eye does not harmonize with sound, nor the ear with form, and so forth). Blue and yellow suddenly change places; (the visual consciousness is impermanent). Movement and stillness repeatedly shift and distort;
(the auditory consciousness is impermanent). Odors distinguish themselves as fragrance arrives; (the olfactory consciousness is impermanent). Sweetness comes, then the bland follows;

(the gustatory consciousness is impermanent). Heat and cold easily alternate; (the tactile consciousness is impermanent). Like and dislike are always biased and partial; (the mental consciousness is impermanent). When objects perish, where can the mind find rest? Sentiment...
When wisdom is forgotten, even solitude is lonely. One overturns the den of the five desires and crushes the nests of the six sense organs. Robbers submit to the King’s transformation;
birds escape from the net. When shall I awaken to the eternal? May all delusions be utterly extinguished.

Contemplating that all phenomena are without self and that all dharmas arise from conditions, one first asserts the doctrine of no-self. Because of causes and conditions, there is arising and ceasing;

thus, thoughts fluctuate between high and low. What one seeks to gain turns into loss; in seeking leisure, one instead encounters busyness. Fearing the cold winter, one does not cease one's toil; suffering through the heat of summer, it seems even longer.
The poor remember the joy of wealth; the old yearn for the vigor of youth. Who would loathe what is harmonious and pleasant? Who would cherish danger and ruin?

(Gain and loss, leisure and busyness, cold and heat—all arise from conditions and do not depend on me. Only in self-mastery does one become a master. How can flux and change be permanent? When separated from the root, how can thought arise?
Without consciousness, the object vanishes. Within and without, there is not a single thing; what is it that is hidden in the middle? The six windows...
Vast and silent, a single chamber stands exposed and grand. Once the dust of worldly toil is exhausted, one is immediately the Great Awakened King.

When planting a tree, one sighs that it has finally been sown and nurtured; its branches and leaves now flourish with joy. The master loves this fine seedling and irrigates it with exceptional diligence.
Having been nurtured for many years, I daily hoped to ascend the clouds and mist. But with shallow soil and unfirm roots, I was shaken by the assault of wind and rain.
In a single morning, I finally toppled over; my very roots no longer remain. Alas! Alas again! It only serves to increase the sighs of my master.
Inscription on Lan Tianshu’s Painting of the Lotus Buddha-land:
In the Land of the Lotus Buddha, the lotus flowers serve as palaces. The inhabitants of that land are identical in appearance; their father is Amitābha and their elder brother is a Mahāsattva.
They do not grow from milk and nourishment, but are born within the lotuses. The size of the flowers is equal to their bodies, reaching perhaps one or two *li* in diameter.
A hundred *li* away, wondrous fragrances arise within the radiance. With natural purity beyond compare, wisdom is their food and meditative concentration their drink.
The Dharma-body knows neither aging nor illness; the waters of virtue abound and the jeweled ground is level. What need is there for plowing fields or digging wells?
That Buddha’s power of aspiration is uniquely transcendent; he does not exclude even those who commit the five heinous crimes or the ten evil deeds. Faith and aspiration—
If one holds the Name without fail, in future years one will surely be reborn upon the Lotus. Master Lan has exquisitely mastered the principles of painting;
the myriad layers of the Buddha-realm are revealed from his brush. The entire Dharma-realm is contained within a single sheet of paper, such that one is unaware of the vast space remaining.

I observe that the Pure Land is a true painting; for your sake, I shall explain it clearly and in detail. The physical marks and signs of Amitābha are the painted Buddha; the adornment of the seven treasures is the painted land.
The sentient beings of the nine grades are the people within the painting; the four-colored lotus flowers are the seats within the painting.
The arrayed scenes of this painted realm are present before our eyes, yet if one seeks the actual Dharma, it has no fixed location. This is the person who paints, and the Dharma that is painted.
Since there is no reality, it is the same for contemplation and the contemplator. Wondrous contemplation is nothing other than emptiness, provisionality, and the Middle;
it is neither one, nor three, nor two. Together with you, we behold the painted Amitābha and proceed westward into the painted realm.
There we shall personally realize the Land of Peace and Bliss within our own minds, and return once more to deliver the suffering world of Saṃsāra.
A Song of Sacrificing the Body to Pray for Rain (With Preface).
The layman Song Kuixian was a native of Mingzhou. His family resided by the southern gate of the prefecture. In his daily life, he served the Buddha with great sincerity and diligence.
In the summer of the *xinchou* year, there was a severe drought; the prayers offered by the prefectures and counties were all without response. He spoke to others, saying: "I shall..."
He proceeded to the Dragon Pool on Tianjing Mountain and cast himself down into it. In an instant, rain poured down in torrents;
it ceased only after ten days, and the people relied upon it for their security. When the lay practitioner first sacrificed his body, he asked the way from a monk at Tianjing Temple.
As the monk watched him depart, he saw clouds arise from the sky, and after a short while, the rain began to pour from all sides. The monk [was moved].
Suspecting this, he went to investigate and saw the layman sitting cross-legged upon the water, solemn and motionless.
He then informed his family, who took the body back for burial. Alas, how extraordinary!

In the past, when our World-Honored One practiced the path of a bodhisattva, he sacrificed his body countless times to save sentient beings and thereby attained Buddhahood. Now, observing the deeds of this layman, [one sees a similar resolve].
If such a person is indeed like this yet is not called a Bodhisattva, I do not believe it. Thus, I have composed a long song to record it:
In the summer of the year Xin-chou, the drought demon was arrogant; the parching heat acted with cruelty as if burning everything down. Heaven and earth became a furnace, and the sun—
Charcoal! It scorches all things until they wither and blacken. The golden sun blazes so fiercely that feathers are singed; the fiery clouds flare up, never ceasing.
From summer to autumn, fifty days have passed, yet not a drop of rain is heard to moisten the rice seedlings. The fields and the earth are all split asunder;
rivers, streams, and brooks are filled with rising dust and clamor. Even the frog at the bottom of the well cannot find solace in its own concealment.
The fish in the living pond—how can their lives escape? The farmers cry out in distress, their voices wailing. They call to Heaven but hear no response; they resent the heavens for being so high.

Their coarse cloth trousers are worn through to bare flesh; the grain in the fields has withered, leaving not even a weed to be seen. At this time, the magistrates of the commanderies and counties have no plan left;
they pray for rain for the people, their hearts filled with anxiety. They summon spirits and dispatch ghosts, yet none can respond; the sorcerers recite their incantations...
The artifice was without merit; how marvelous that the Great Being, for the sake of sentient beings, went directly to the Dragon Palace to summon the slumbering dragon.
The old dragon, his midday nap not yet satisfied, was startled awake and overturned the waves upon the level plain. How surging flows the water of the dragon pool!
Beneath it, the soft-shelled turtles and crocodiles constantly roar in fury. He cast himself straight down ten thousand feet, and suddenly surged back up to the surface like—
Floating gourds drift upon the water; after ten days of rain, it finally ceases. Villages, plains, cities, and markets are all surrounded by the waters;
the dead are revived and the withered are moistened. The ripening grain and millet seem to overturn the rivers, and boats on the wild fields unknowingly enter the city.
A gentle oar suddenly reaches the gate and rocks there. The weary find rest and the sick rise up. Country folk congratulate one another and neighbors invite one another; they sigh in wonderment.

Ah! To the ordinary person, the Great Being is unfathomable; children and women constantly mock him. Yet, when he seeks to save the world, he sacrifices his own body and life, regarding the four great elements as being no different from bubbles on water.
The suffering of sentient beings is his own suffering; how could there be even a hair’s breadth of distinction between self and others?
He desires only that all may attain peace and happiness; though his body suffers and his heart is pained, his spirit remains joyful. Thus have I heard of this man.
There is indeed such a thing as death; some regard it as heavy as Mount Tai, while others deem it lighter than a goose’s down.
This rain does not descend from the Dragon King, nor is it the tide of rivers and seas; it emerges directly from the compassionate heart of the Great Being (Mahāsattva).

Every drop and every particle is transformed into the fat, marrow, blood, flesh, life-force, and vitality of sentient beings. It enables the cold to be clothed, the hungry to eat, the chaotic to be governed, and the rebellious to be subdued. Yellow...
Gold is not yet considered precious; how can white jade be deemed noble? The Great Being does not accept merit—where, then, could such merit be inscribed?
I have composed this song-poem to record these events, leaving it as a chant to be sung for ten thousand autumns and ten thousand ages.

Two Poems Presented to the Layman of Dong'e The man of tranquility south of the city dwells high, reclining upon a single bed of books. What worldly affairs have I? My mind is purified, remaining simply at ease.
Bending my waist, I cease begging for rice; plucking at the strings, I do not seek fish. Day and night we visit one another, as the autumn wind fills my humble thatched cottage.

Tranquil and aloof, I decline the company of my contemporaries; carefree, I stay far from the marketplace. Dividing the spring water, I briefly irrigate the chrysanthemums; filling in the paintings, I gaze upon the mountains. To have affection is to fall into a vice;
only when there is no seeking does one become truly at ease. There is no need to turn with the shifting objects of the world; awaken to the truth right where you are, and there is nowhere to return.
About to depart for Zhejiang, I leave this parting verse for the Layman of Shuofang, an old remnant from the Society of the Far Field:
Meeting beyond the mundane world, we speak of past causes. A thousand li of passes and mountains, two weary travelers.
Half a ladle of wind and moon, one idle body. A small boat in fine rain, a solitary lamp at night; Residual snow and cold plum blossoms in antiquity.
Temple Spring. I intend to cultivate pure deeds next year, to become a fellow practitioner with you in planting lotuses.

The water-strainer, as a means of protecting living beings, is the most difficult to maintain; you should practice these subtle observances without laxity. Life and death have always been beyond one's control.
Small! From this point on, birth and death intersect. If even a single hair is removed from the body one knows the pain; how can one bear to consume a full cup that fills the belly?
I urge all travelers to be most careful: every morning, you must diligently inspect your water for insects.
An Account of Paying Homage at the Stūpa, Eight Poems (with Preface).

In the third month of spring in the year Jihai, I crossed the river from Xiling and traveled to Ayuwang Mountain in Siming to pay homage to the precious stūpa containing the true-body relics of Śākyamuni Tathāgata.
There I encountered Master Dejian, who was performing his devotions at the temple.

The period for circumambulating the stūpa was set to reach eighty-four thousand times. I remained behind to join them in their prostrations. Delighted, I proceeded to that place and spent the summer retreat there.
After more than a month, I heard that this Great Master had also arrived; we performed our circumambulations at the same time.

Beyond our daily recitations, the three of us discussed the Buddha-dharma, finding great joy in one another’s company and regretting only that we had met so late. We observed the *an-ju* (summer retreat).
When it was finished, I lit one finger as an offering to the Buddha and composed a poem to record this event, so as to manifest the sublime essence of that moment:
Two thousand years since the Parinirvāṇa of Kāśyapa, The śarīra remains resplendent even now. I rejoice in what virtuous deeds I must have performed in past lives.

It is beneficial. While visiting the gate of the Zhan Guangxiang Pagoda, I saw a single object like a pearl attached to a small bell; blue, yellow, red, and white appeared in endless variety. This is one's own mind perceiving the marks of its own mind;
it is not the form of the Tathāgata, for they are not the same.
The Buddha-body is fundamentally without birth or extinction; from where, then, could the śarīra have come? When the True Buddha appears before one’s face, one errs;
falsely employing discrimination, one is startled and suspicious.
The Hall contains the precious stupa, and the stupa contains space; in every land and within every atom, all are fundamentally integrated. Eighty thousand are neither many nor one;
upon the tip of a single hair, the Palace of the Jewel King appears.
Our Buddha cultivated merit and wisdom for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas; his achievement is complete, and his enduring legacy is seen through the ages.
This single seed of luminosity within ourselves has long been buried in the dust until this very day.
Six times a day I fix my thoughts to pay homage to the King of Emptiness; I repent with such earnestness that I never forget for a moment.
When the moon rises above the spire of the stupa and people have awakened from sleep, one suspects that the śarīra is emitting rays of light.
Though the King of Physicians has departed, his medicine remains; yet this shameless, deluded child’s illness is not yet healed.
Having finished reading the "Exhortation to Uphold the Teachings" chapter of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, my heart is grieved and tears flow uncontrollably.
As summer ends, with what shall I serve the Buddha? Holding up a single finger, I shall burn it as a lamp. Yet there remains the ignorance that has not been consumed;
it does not vanish all at once along with the lingering embers.
In the third month of the spring of the Gengxu year, I observed the *jinzu* (foot-binding) retreat at the western courtyard of Fantian Temple.
I named my room on the right side of the hall "Cunxiang Zhai" (The Inch-Perfume Studio). When honored guests visited me there, we would briefly exchange a few words of dharma discourse.
Aside from a pinch of incense, there is nothing but the recitation of the Buddha’s name. I have composed this poem to manifest my resolve and announce to the assembly:

Master Xing has sold his property to construct a Zen chamber; the ancient temple is reopened as a Hall of Pure Practice. He has swept away all worldly attachments like spit and saliva, relying solely on the four characters [Namo Amitābha] as his provisions for the journey.
Together with fellow practitioners, we shall form a society for three years; facing the world, there remains only this one [vow].
A pinch of incense. My samādhi has not yet reached fruition or maturity; in this life, I shall never reach the city wall.

Having spontaneously composed these four verses, I realize I have no choice but to dwell in the deep mountains. My single chamber is desolate as I alone close the gate. I send word to the people of the world: do not look upon me.
Summoned! This life shall never again reach the human realm.
With this rosary of one hundred and eight beads and the six-syllable mantra, I shall spend my years and pass through my days;
throughout my entire life, I have had only the vow to return to the West—how could I bear to let this heart be burdened by external conditions?
In practicing virtue, people are diligent at the outset but few can persevere to the end; I vow to be single-minded and perfect my observance of the precepts throughout my life.
From this day forward, once the shadow has passed the meridian, not even a grain of rice shall enter my mouth.
To rescue those drowning from a shattered boat is logically impossible; one must row with all one's might until reaching the shore.
Once the helmsman has helped everyone ashore, he would surely take up a new oar and enter the middle of the stream once more.

In the six characters of "Nianfo Shuohuai" (Expressing My Feelings on Mindfulness of the Buddha), there is not a single superfluous dharma. In an ordinary moment, I have seen through the barrier of the Patriarchs. Zhaozhou did not delight in it, yet I personally do;
from now on, this public case must be overturned once more.

Departing from this world, the body remains amidst the flowers as the Buddha appears before one. The Buddha’s light shines forth upon the purple-gold lotus; the mind follows the Buddhas to be reborn there.
Within the state of neither coming nor going, all matters are perfectly manifest.
Biography of Master Sheng’an (Appendix) The Master’s name was Shi-xian;
his courtesy name was Si-qi, and he was also styled Sheng’an. He was the son of the Shi family of Changshu, whose lineage had been engaged in the study of Confucianism for generations.

From birth, the Master abstained from meat. While still a youth with his hair tied in a topknot, he harbored a resolve to transcend the mundane world. After his father passed away early, his mother, Lady Zhang, recognized [his inclinations].
Having long cultivated roots of goodness, he was ordained as a son of the Śākya clan at the age of seven. He took Sengrong of the Qingliang Hermitage as his preceptor;
he was intelligent, sagacious, and clear-headed, and he never forgot a single word of the scriptures upon reading them once. At fifteen, he shaved his head and received the full precepts.

He was well-versed in secular classics, capable of composing poetry, and skilled in calligraphy. Senior contemporaries such as Qian Yuyou and Xu Yanggu both esteemed his integrity and befriended him; yet, he never...

In an instant, he forgot the great matter of life and death. By nature, he was deeply filial. When his mother passed away, he knelt before a Buddha image and recited the *Bao’en Jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness).
During the seven-week mourning period and on annual festivals such as the伏 (*fu*) and 臘 (*la*), he invariably set up images and prepared offerings.

Later, while at Puren Temple, he saw a monk die and fall to the ground; the Master was struck with sudden realization of the impermanence of the world and redoubled his efforts. He reached the age of twenty-four.

Yuan Shi-luo resided at Zhaokong Temple, where he strictly practiced the Vinaya. He never parted from his robes and alms bowl, limited himself to a single meal per day, and did not lie down with his side touching the mat;
these were his regular practices. In the year Gengyin, he followed Dharma Master Qucheng to hear lectures on the *Lotus Sūtra* and its perfect meaning (*yuan-yi*).

He also visited Dharma Master Shaotán to study various treatises, including the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and the *Zhi guan*. He investigated these texts day and night, and before three summers had passed, he had mastered them.
He thoroughly mastered the principles of the Three Contemplations and Ten Vehicles, as well as the studies of Nature and Characteristics (Xingxiang).

Master Tan then conferred upon him the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), transmitting to him the orthodox lineage of Tiantai through four generations from Lingfeng. In the year Jiawu, he visited Master Lingju at Chongfu Temple.

He took up the koan "Investigate 'Who is this that recites the Buddha's name? with rigorous discipline. In the fourth month, he attained a sudden and profound realization, exclaiming, "I have awakened from my dream.

From then on, his responses to situations were unimpeded and his eloquence was masterful and versatile. When Nanyue wished to entrust him with the robe and whisk, he did not accept them and took his leave.
Thereupon, he confined himself at Zhenji Temple, reading the Sanskrit volumes of the Tripiṭaka by day and reciting the names of the Buddhas of the Western Paradise by night.

When the three-year period was completed, the monastic community of the temple requested that he lecture on the *Lotus Sūtra*. As the Master ascended the seat to expound it, the river surged and the springs gushed forth;
the flow was so copious that it could not be resisted. In the first spring of the Wuxu year, he stayed at Longxing Temple in Hangzhou.

At the command of Dharma Master Shao Tan, the Master took his place to lecture on the *Sūtras* and the *Vinaya*, for which the Dharma Master repeatedly beat time and praised him as excellent. In the spring of the Jihai year, he traveled to Mount Ayuwang in Siming to pay homage.
Śāriputra, for five years prior and subsequent [to this], he burned his fingers as incense in offering to the Buddha.

Every year on the anniversary of the Buddha’s Parinirvāṇa, he lectured on the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* and the *Amitābha-sūtra*, demonstrating the principle that "this mind is the Buddha. He universally encompassed those of the three faculties, and the influence of his Dharma spread far and wide.

Monastics and laypeople throughout Jiangsu and Zhejiang turned their hearts toward him in devotion. Ten years have passed since, and the grandeur of his Dharma assemblies has been preeminent among all regions. Furthermore—

He once served at various Chan monasteries, including Yongfu, Pujing, and Haiyun. Each time he entered a monastery, he established a new standard for its model; the monastic regulations were solemn and dignified.

Daily, he lectured on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Śūraṃgama-samādhi-sūtra*, and other scriptures, and those who held up their texts to inquire about difficult points gathered in great numbers beneath his seat.
Not long after, he withdrew to seclusion at Xianlin Temple in Hangzhou, where he did not leave his quarters and diligently cultivated the Pure Land practice. In the winter of the Jiyou year, Hang...
Rén Mào, Jìngyuǎn, Yè Shēng, Huángfù Ziyí, and Lǐ Zhíyù, along with the monastery administrators Shěnggōng and Yīwěi, invited him to preside over Fàntián Jiǎngsì on Mount Fèngshān.
Thereupon, he severed all external entanglements and focused exclusively on the Pure Land. He established long-term retreats and strictly formulated monastic regulations;
throughout the six periods of day and night, they exhorted one another, leading everyone to say that Yongming had appeared once more.

He arrived. He served as the abbot of the monastery for over ten years. Among his disciples who received ordination, as well as those who sought the precepts and took refuge, there were several hundred.
Occasionally, there were those who studied poetry and prose; the Master sternly admonished them, saying: "Human life lasts but a breath.
How can one afford the leisure to study worldly texts? A single moment of negligence, and one has already entered the next world. If you wish to transcend [suffering]..."

He was free from all calamities indeed. On the day the Buddha attained enlightenment—the *guichou* (癸丑) day—he said to his disciples, "I shall depart for eternity on the fourteenth day of the fourth month next year.
From that time forth, he closed his quarters and maintained a fast with every inch of incense, limiting himself to reciting the Buddha’s name one hundred thousand times each day and night.
On the second day of the fourth month of the following year, the *jiayin* (甲寅) year, he emerged from his seclusion. On the twelfth day, he addressed the assembly, saying, "My ten..."
"I saw the Three Sages of the West descend into the void the other day; now I see them again. Shall I be reborn in the Pure Land?

Thus he spoke, and immediately entrusted the affairs of the monastery to his successors. He then took leave of all the lay patrons throughout the city. A servant requested that the Master compose a verse, which he wrote as follows:
"The body dwells within the lotus, and the Buddha appears before me; The Buddha’s light shines upon this purple-gold lotus. My mind follows the Buddhas as they depart."
He departed. Amidst the absence of coming and going, the events unfolded clearly. Having finished writing, he said, "I shall certainly attain rebirth on the fourteenth day.

You all should assemble for me to practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation). On the thirteenth day, he ceased taking food and drink. He closed his eyes and sat upright. At the fifth watch, he bathed and changed his robes.
Facing west, he sat in the full lotus posture. By the hour of *si* (10–12 AM), people from near and far had gathered like clouds; they wept with snow-like tears and prostrated themselves, saying:
"I pray that you, Master, remain in this world to deliver sentient beings. The Master opened his eyes again and said, "I shall depart and then return.

The matter of birth and death is great; each of you should purify your minds and recite the Buddha's name. Having spoken these words, he joined his palms, invoked the Buddha’s name, and passed away. A short while later, his nose-cord hung down.
The color [of the remains] was bright and lustrous; even until the enshrinement in the stupa chamber, the color did not change.
On the eighth day of the twelfth month of that year, the senior monk Wuzhu of Yushan enshrined the sacred relics and interred them in a pagoda at Fushiyan on the western side of Qinchuan.

On the fifteenth day of the second month of the seventh year of the Qianlong era, the monastics and laypeople of Mount Meo, cherishing the Master’s spiritual conduct, escorted the relics away and rebuilt the pagoda.
To the right of Yuwang Temple stands his former stupa, which is said to enshrine his robes and alms bowl.

The Master was born on the eighth day of the eighth month in the twenty-fourth year of the Kangxi era. He lived to the age of forty-nine and maintained twenty-five years of monastic seniority (*śrāmaṇera*).

He composed one hundred and eight verses on the Pure Land, annotated the *Western Vow Text*, compiled the *Continued Biographies of Those Reborn*, and wrote the *Commentary on the Eastern Sea*. His relics are preserved here.

The various repentance rituals for *nirvāṇa* have all been practiced in the world. On the Double Ninth day of the year of Yi-chou (1745), during the Qianlong reign, my fellow student Xī'ān Lǜrán composed this in the right-wing hall of the Jìzhào Hall at Sānfēng.

The text on the Bodhicitta describes a vast and great compassionate heart. The Forty-Eight Vows possess profound and deep power; their transformative guidance is earnest and sincere.

He cultivated diligence with such intensity that scholars of pure conduct heard of his reputation and held him in profound esteem. To this day, nearly ninety years later, people still praise him without ceasing.
His practice and realization were authentic, and his auspicious responses were transcendent. Even placed among the great masters of a thousand or ten thousand years, he stands towering and eminent.
Is it not fitting, then, that he be honored as a true successor to the orthodox patriarchs of a generation?

Elder Master Yong of Huaru Chan Monastery, who is doubly accomplished in both the Chan and Pure Land traditions—
Quan fully reveals the esoteric and the manifest, urging himself toward diligent effort with a sincere heart for others.

Beyond his practice of meditation and recitation, he delights in taking up the words and phrases of Master Xingxue to admonish students. This spring, he reprinted and circulated them; one can see a glimpse of his vow to liberate himself and others.
Having completed the publication, he showed it to me and requested that I verify the erroneous characters; thus, I have recorded this "Huo Ran" (Sudden Enlightenment) preface.
I have composed these verses of praise as a postscript to the *Biographies of the Nine Patriarchs of the Lotus School* written by Master Kaigong.

By means of this small portion of merit, I pray that Master Yong and all those—whether monastics or laypeople—who read this book from now until the end of time, shall together with [Master] Yong attain non-retrogressive bodhi and be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). May Master Xing serve as witness within the eternal light of the *dharmadhātu*.
